0.title: The Throne of Grace: The Book of 2 Samuel
0.overview:
Second Samuel is the story of a king — but it is more profoundly the story of a covenant. At its center stands the most important promise in the entire Old Testament: I will establish the throne of his kingdom forever (7:13). The Davidic covenant is the theological spine of 2 Samuel, and everything before it (David's painful, glorious consolidation of the kingdom) and everything after it (the catastrophic sins, the rebellions, the griefs of his later years) must be read in its light. God's covenant with David is unconditional, permanent, and eschatological — it will not be broken by David's failures or by his successors' failures, because it rests on the character of God, not the character of David.

The book divides naturally into three movements. The first (chapters 1–10) traces the arc of David's rise: the lament for Saul and Jonathan, the seven-year civil war, the coronation as king of all Israel, the conquest of Jerusalem, the tumultuous bringing of the ark to the city of David, and the great covenant of chapter 7. These are the years of unambiguous triumph, and even here the narrative is honest: the ark kills Uzzah; Michal's contempt ends her marriage; David's wars, however just, are also costly. But the dominant note is grace — the shepherd boy from Bethlehem, anointed in the sight of his brothers, now sits on the throne of a united Israel and receives the most extraordinary promise ever spoken to a human being.

The second movement (chapters 11–20) is the great unraveling. David sees Bathsheba, takes her, commits adultery, arranges Uriah's murder, and lives in self-deception for perhaps a year until Nathan arrives with a parable and a verdict: You are the man. His repentance — recorded in Psalm 51 — is the deepest and most honest in the OT, and it stands in permanent contrast to Saul's self-justification. But the consequences are real and devastating: the child dies, Amnon rapes Tamar, Absalom murders Amnon and launches a coup, and David flees Jerusalem weeping, barefoot, ascending the Mount of Olives — one of the most heartbreaking scenes in all of Scripture, and one of the most Christ-haunted.

The third movement (chapters 21–24) is a kind of appendix: poems, lists, and a final plague that ends at the threshing floor of Araunah — the very site where Solomon will build the temple, where Abraham offered Isaac, where the intersection of divine judgment and divine mercy is most concentrated in all of human history. The book ends not with David's triumph but with his sacrifice, and with the mercy that stops the destroying angel above Jerusalem. It is, in miniature, the grammar of the entire gospel.

Christologically, 2 Samuel is inexhaustible. The Davidic covenant of chapter 7 is the direct seedbed of the NT's proclamation that Jesus is the Son of David (Matt. 1:1; Luke 1:32–33; Rom. 1:3; Rev. 22:16). Mephibosheth's story (chapter 9) is one of the OT's most perfect pictures of grace — the crippled heir of a dead dynasty, brought to the king's table, not because of what he was but because of the covenant David made with his father Jonathan. David's lament over Absalom — O my son Absalom, my son, my son Absalom! Would I had died instead of you (18:33) — is the cry of a father for a son who died in rebellion, and it reaches across the centuries to the Father who gave his Son for those who were at war with him. And the final threshing-floor sacrifice, where David insists on paying for what he offers — I will not offer burnt offerings to the LORD my God that cost me nothing (24:24) — is the eternal principle of substitutionary sacrifice: the offering must cost the one who offers it.

1.title: The Lament of the Bow
1.text: <sup>19</sup>'Your glory, O Israel, is slain on your high places! How the mighty have fallen! <sup>26</sup>I am distressed for you, my brother Jonathan; very pleasant have you been to me; your love to me was extraordinary, surpassing the love of women. <sup>27</sup>How the mighty have fallen, and the weapons of war perished!' (ESV)
1.overview:
Second Samuel opens not with a coronation but with a lament. The news of Saul's death — and Jonathan's — arrives in Ziklag, carried by an Amalekite who has added a self-incriminating lie to the truth, apparently thinking David will reward him for finishing off the king who had been pursuing him. He miscalculates catastrophically: David tears his clothes, mourns, fasts, and then executes the messenger for claiming to have killed the LORD's anointed. The man who refused to raise his hand against Saul in life will not celebrate Saul's death.

The theological center of the chapter is not the execution but the lament — the poem David composes for Saul and Jonathan, called the Lament of the Bow (v. 18), one of the supreme pieces of Hebrew poetry. It is remarkable in what it does not do: it does not condemn Saul, does not vindicate David, does not mention God's judgment on a disobedient king. It simply grieves. It mourns Saul's genuine greatness alongside Jonathan's extraordinary love. This is the heart of the man after God's own heart: wide enough, gracious enough, to honor what was genuinely honorable in the man who tried to murder him. David does not wait until it is safe to mourn; he leads the mourning before anyone knows what his position will be.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: An Amalekite arrives from the battle of Gilboa claiming to have killed Saul at the king's own request. David's response is grief, not relief — and execution, not reward. The man who thought he was bringing good news to a fugitive finds himself before a king who honors the Lord's anointed above his own survival.
verseByVerse.theology: David's execution of the Amalekite is not vengeance but covenantal principle: the LORD's anointed is inviolable, regardless of whether that anointing has been functionally vacated. The office retains its dignity until God himself removes its occupant.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Amalekite's logic was entirely reasonable on human terms — David had been fleeing Saul for years. Now: The person who expects the Christian to celebrate the downfall of an enemy, even a genuine one, misunderstands the character that grace produces. The ability to grieve the loss of a genuine opponent is a mark of spiritual largeness.

verseByVerse.quote: After the death of Saul, when David had returned from striking down the Amalekites, David remained two days in Ziklag. And on the third day, behold, a man came from Saul's camp, with his clothes torn and dirt on his head. And when he came to David, he fell to the ground and paid homage. David said to him, 'Where do you come from?' And he said to him, 'I have escaped from the camp of Israel.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The timing is significant: David has just returned from the disaster and rescue at Ziklag (chapter 30), and two days into his recovery a messenger arrives from Gilboa. The torn clothes and dirt on the head are the ancient signs of mourning and crisis — the messenger is signaling before he speaks that the news is catastrophic. The structure of the opening inquiry — where do you come from? what happened? — is almost formal, a legal proceeding in miniature. David wants the facts before he responds.

The Amalekite's identity is no accident. The last time David encountered Amalekites was at Ziklag, where they raided his city and took his wives captive. And the last great command concerning Amalek was Saul's failure to execute the herem in chapter 15 — the command that cost him his kingdom. Now an Amalekite arrives claiming to have killed the king who refused to kill Amalek. The narrative's irony is dark and precise: the nation Saul refused to destroy destroys Saul. R. C. Sproul notes that the judgment deferred is not the judgment canceled — it simply arrives by a different route and at a higher cost.

verseByVerse.quote: And David said to him, 'How do you know that Saul and his son Jonathan are dead?' And the young man who told him said, 'By chance I happened to be on Mount Gilboa, and there was Saul leaning on his spear, and behold, the chariots and the horsemen were close upon him. And he said to me, Use your sword, and thrust me through with it... So I stood beside him and killed him, because I knew that he could not live after he had fallen.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Amalekite's account contradicts chapter 31's account of Saul's death — there, Saul fell on his own sword after his armor-bearer refused; here, the Amalekite claims he finished the king at Saul's own request. Most commentators conclude the Amalekite is lying, perhaps looting the battlefield and taking the crown and bracelet from Saul's already-dead body, and constructing a story he thinks will earn reward from David. If so, it is one of the most catastrophically misjudged calculations in the book.

But whether true or false, the claim requires the same response from David: the anointed of the LORD has died, and the man standing before him claims responsibility. Alistair Begg observes that the Amalekite's error was a misunderstanding of David's character so complete that he had clearly built his expectation of David on the wrong foundation — on what he thought David wanted rather than on what David actually valued. Many people make the same mistake with God: they assume God shares their priorities, their preferences, their standards of success. The Amalekite thought David wanted Saul dead. He was profoundly, fatally wrong.

verseByVerse.quote: Then David took hold of his clothes and tore them, and so did all the men who were with him. And they mourned and wept and fasted until evening for Saul and for Jonathan his son and for the people of the LORD and for the house of Israel, because they had fallen by the sword. And David said to the young man who told him, 'How is it you were not afraid to put out your hand to destroy the LORD's anointed?' And David called one of the young men and said, 'Go, execute him.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
David's mourning is immediate, corporate, and genuine. He does not calculate his public image; he tears his clothes and leads his men in fasting and weeping until evening. This is not political theater — it is the authentic response of a man whose best friend is dead and whose king, however flawed, has fallen. The list of those mourned is significant: Saul, Jonathan, the people of the LORD, the house of Israel. David does not mourn his personal loss alone; he mourns the national catastrophe, the loss to Israel as a whole.

The execution of the Amalekite on the principle — your own mouth testified against you, saying, I have killed the LORD's anointed — is not judicial excess but covenantal clarity. David has just spent six chapters refusing to touch the LORD's anointed, at personal cost, on theological principle. He cannot now reward someone who claims to have done what he refused to do. The principle must be consistent: the LORD's anointed is inviolable. What David would not do for his own survival, no one else may do for his benefit. Calvin notes that David's consistency here — maintaining the same theological standard toward Saul dead that he maintained toward Saul alive — is the evidence that the principle was genuine and not merely expedient.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 17–27 — The Lament of the Bow
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: David's lament for Saul and Jonathan is Hebrew poetry at its most refined — three stanzas moving from public grief to personal anguish, mourning Saul's genuine greatness and Jonathan's extraordinary love without theological commentary or self-vindication.
verseByVerse.theology: The poem's silence about God — unusual in David's poetry — is itself a theological statement: in the raw grief of loss, David does not theologize; he mourns. The ability to grieve without immediately reaching for explanation is a form of faith. Grief that honors what was truly good in the one who has died is a covenant grace.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The poem was to be taught to the people of Judah (v. 18) — David wanted the nation to learn this lament, to hold the grief communally, to honor the fallen king alongside his own joy at accession. Now: The Christian practice of honest, full grief — neither suppressed by premature comfort nor prolonged by refusal of hope — images the grief of David who could mourn his enemy and of the Father who grieves the lost.

verseByVerse.quote: And David lamented with this lamentation over Saul and Jonathan his son, and he said it should be taught to the people of Judah; behold, it is written in the Book of Jashar.
verseByVerse.commentary: Before the lament itself begins, these verses establish its solemnity and its reach. David does not simply grieve privately - he composes a formal lament and orders it taught to the people of Judah. This is grief institutionalized, grief made communal, grief given theological weight. A king has fallen; his people must feel it together. The reference to the Book of Jashar - an ancient collection of heroic poetry also cited in Joshua 10:13 - signals that David's lament belongs to a recognized tradition of honoring Israel's great figures. The lament of the bow is named for the weapon Saul and Jonathan wielded, and these verses prepare us to receive it as more than personal sorrow. It is a national act of mourning, a liturgy of loss. Calvin observes that David's command to teach the lament to Judah reveals his pastoral instinct even in grief: the people need to process this loss together, and their king will lead them in doing so.

verseByVerse.quote: 'Your glory, O Israel, is slain on your high places! How the mighty have fallen! Tell it not in Gath, publish it not in the streets of Ashkelon, lest the daughters of the Philistines rejoice, lest the daughters of the uncircumcised exult. You mountains of Gilboa, let there be no dew or rain upon you... Saul and Jonathan, beloved and lovely! In life and in death they were not divided; they were swifter than eagles; they were stronger than lions.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Tell it not in Gath — the refrain has entered the language as a proverb for things too shameful or painful to be broadcast to enemies. David's instinct is to protect the honor of Israel even in the moment of its greatest humiliation. This is covenantal solidarity: the defeat is Israel's defeat, and even now David does not capitalize on it. He is thinking as Israel's king before he has been publicly crowned as such.

The description of Saul and Jonathan — beloved and lovely, in life and in death not divided, swifter than eagles, stronger than lions — is genuinely and generously honorific. It does not rewrite history; it identifies what was genuinely true about these men at their best. Saul was a warrior; Jonathan was a hero; both were beloved to Israel; both died together on Gilboa. David can hold this truth without qualification, which is itself evidence of his greatness. Tim Keller writes that the capacity to honor what is genuinely honorable in someone who has opposed you is one of the clearest marks of a soul whose security does not depend on the diminishment of others. David has nothing to prove by diminishing Saul; he is already the LORD's anointed. From that security, he can be fully, honestly generous.

verseByVerse.quote: 'How the mighty have fallen in the midst of the battle! Jonathan lies slain on your high places. I am distressed for you, my brother Jonathan; very pleasant have you been to me; your love to me was extraordinary, surpassing the love of women. How the mighty have fallen, and the weapons of war perished!'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The poem ends where grief always ends — with the personal. Saul has been honored as king and warrior; now David turns to Jonathan, and the poetry becomes intimate: I am distressed for you, my brother Jonathan. The word for distressed (tzar) means pressed, confined, as if grief has narrowed the whole world to this loss. Jonathan's love — extraordinary, surpassing the love of women — is not a romantic declaration but a covenant one: the kind of love Jonathan showed was more costly, more deliberate, more theologically grounded than anything even the deepest romantic love usually requires. Jonathan gave up his inheritance, his crown, his proximity to power, his safety — for David. No woman in David's life had been asked to give up so much.

Sinclair Ferguson observes that the lament ends with the weapons of war perished — not with a call to vengeance or a promise of military restoration, but with the image of war itself having run its terrible course. The chapter opens 2 Samuel at the register of grief rather than triumph, which is exactly right: the kingdom David will build is being constructed on the grave of his best friend and his predecessor. Every throne rests on someone's suffering. The throne David inherits will eventually point to the throne of his greater Son, who entered his kingdom through a cross.

1.theology:
Grieving Well as a Covenant Grace. Chapter 1 establishes from the first page that David's kingship will be characterized not by self-promotion but by covenant loyalty — including the hardest form of covenant loyalty, which is honoring the genuinely honorable in those who opposed you. The lament is not just a personal expression; it is a theological act. It refuses the cheap grace of pretending Saul's death was simply good news, or that Jonathan's death was an acceptable collateral cost of David's coronation. Both deaths are mourned at full weight.

The LORD's Anointed and the Cost of Principle. David's execution of the Amalekite is the hinge between 1 Samuel's theology and 2 Samuel's: the same principle that kept David from killing Saul in the cave, in the camp, and at every opportunity through the fugitive years is now applied consistently in the context of power. Principles held only when they are costly are genuine principles; principles abandoned as soon as they become inconvenient are mere tactics. David passes the test.
1.examples:
Then: The lament was commanded to be taught in Judah (v. 18) — a deliberate act of communal formation. David wanted Israel's grief over Saul to be structured, honest, and generous, because the kind of king he intended to be required a people formed in the same covenant generosity.

Now: The chapter confronts the contemporary instinct to celebrate the downfall of those who have opposed us — even when their downfall is genuinely just. David's lament models the Christian practice of blessing enemies, honoring what was genuinely good in those who failed, and refusing to use another person's ruin for personal advantage. It is the way of the cross before the cross.

2.title: Two Kings in Israel
2.text: <sup>1</sup>After this David inquired of the LORD, 'Shall I go up into any of the cities of Judah?' And the LORD said to him, 'Go up.' David said, 'Where shall I go up?' And he said, 'To Hebron.' <sup>4</sup>And the men of Judah came, and there they anointed David king over the house of Judah. (ESV)
2.overview:
Chapter 2 opens a new era and immediately shows the gap between David's pattern and Saul's pattern: David's first act as potential king is to inquire of the LORD. He does not assume; he asks. And the divine direction is specific: not just Judah, but Hebron — the city of Abraham's burial, the ancient covenant center of the southern tribes. The anointing at Hebron is David's third anointing: first privately by Samuel, then again among his men at Ziklag (implied), now publicly by the tribe of Judah. God's confirmations multiply as the time for the kingdom's arrival approaches.

But the chapter also shows that the kingdom does not come without conflict. Abner, Saul's general, installs Ish-bosheth (Saul's surviving son) as king over the northern tribes — a counter-coronation that fractures Israel for seven and a half years. The civil war between the house of Saul and the house of David is not ideological; it is dynastic, driven primarily by Abner's political interests rather than genuine support for Ish-bosheth, who is described as a weak and pliant figure throughout. The chapter ends with a skirmish at the pool of Gibeon that illustrates the fratricidal tragedy of the civil war: Israelites killing Israelites, brothers chasing brothers across the fields of Benjamin, grief compounding grief.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: David inquires of the LORD and is directed to Hebron. The men of Judah anoint him king. He sends a message of covenant loyalty to the men of Jabesh-gilead, honoring them for burying Saul and declaring his own intentions toward them.
verseByVerse.theology: David's first act as king — asking God — establishes the governing principle of his best years. The kingdom built on divine direction will be sustained by divine direction; the kingdom that replaces inquiry with assumption will eventually collapse. This is the anti-Saul pattern from the first verse.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Hebron was the city where Abraham bought the cave of Machpelah (Gen. 23) — a covenant city, a burial place, a place where the patriarchal promises had been anchored. David's coronation there links the Davidic kingdom to the Abrahamic promises. Now: The believing leader who begins every significant decision with genuine prayer — not as ritual but as actual dependence — is building on the only foundation that holds.

verseByVerse.quote: After this David inquired of the LORD, 'Shall I go up into any of the cities of Judah?' And the LORD said to him, 'Go up.' David said, 'Where shall I go up?' And he said, 'To Hebron.' So David went up there, and his two wives also... And the men of Judah came, and there they anointed David king over the house of Judah.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The chapter's opening — after this David inquired of the LORD — is the most important four words of the chapter. After the grief of chapter 1, after the execution of the Amalekite, after the lament, David does not simply assume it is time to claim the throne. He asks. The inquiry through the ephod (the priestly means of discerning God's will, which Abiathar had carried since chapter 21) returns a directive, and David follows it. He does not negotiate with the directive — he does not say Hebron seems strategic, but perhaps Jerusalem would be better. He obeys the specific word and goes to the specific place.

The anointing by the men of Judah is the public confirmation of what God decreed privately at Bethlehem in 1 Samuel 16. The oil Samuel poured on a shepherd boy in a family home is now enacted publicly before a tribe. And immediately David extends covenantal generosity to the men of Jabesh-gilead — the people who honored Saul's body after Gilboa. His message is both pastoral and political: may the LORD show steadfast love and faithfulness to you. And I also will do good to you because you have done this thing. He uses the covenant word — hesed, steadfast love — and promises to be its human channel. The king who received Jonathan's covenant is now extending that covenant quality to others. This is grace reproducing itself.

verseByVerse.quote: And David sent messengers to the men of Jabesh-gilead and said to them, May you be blessed by the LORD, because you showed this loyalty to Saul your lord and buried him. Now may the LORD show steadfast love and faithfulness to you. And I also will do good to you, because you have done this thing.
verseByVerse.commentary: David's first recorded act as king in Hebron is not to consolidate power but to send gratitude to Jabesh-gilead - the men who risked their lives to retrieve and bury Saul's body (1 Sam. 31:11-13). He blesses them in the name of the LORD, credits their act as hesed - the covenant word for steadfast loyalty - and promises to repay their kindness. The closing line notes that the house of Judah has anointed him king: not a threat, but information. He wants Saul's loyalists to know he is not their enemy. Begg notes that David's instinct at the moment of accession is generosity toward those who served his predecessor - a portrait of kingship that honors rather than erases the past. The men of Jabesh-gilead showed hesed to Saul's corpse; David shows hesed to them for it. Covenant loyalty breeds covenant loyalty.

verseByVerse.quote: But Abner the son of Ner, commander of Saul's army, took Ish-bosheth the son of Saul and brought him over to Mahanaim, and he made him king over Gilead and the Ashurites and Jezreel and Ephraim and Benjamin and all Israel. Ish-bosheth, Saul's son, was forty years old when he began to reign over Israel, and he reigned two years. But the house of Judah followed David. And the time that David was king in Hebron over the house of Judah was seven years and six months.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Abner's installation of Ish-bosheth is a political act, not a theological one. Ish-bosheth — whose name means 'man of shame,' perhaps a later substitution for his original name Eshbaal, 'man of Baal' — is a cipher in the narrative: he appears, makes one complaint, and is murdered in his bed. Abner is the real power behind the counter-throne. He knows the situation is untenable — he will eventually say as much (the LORD has sworn to David... to transfer the kingdom from the house of Saul, 3:9–10) — but dynastic loyalty and personal position keep him in the game for seven years.

The contrast between David's seven years in Hebron (a covenant city, established by divine directive) and Ish-bosheth's two years in Mahanaim (a military camp east of the Jordan, established by Abner's ambition) is the narrator's quiet commentary on the two kingdoms. One is built on God's word; the other is built on a general's calculation. The outcome is not in doubt. R. C. Sproul observes that the seven-year civil war is one of the most theologically painful periods of David's story — not because David is at fault, but because the cost of human rebellion against God's appointed order is always borne by people who did not choose the rebellion. Israel's soldiers die in a war caused by Abner's ambition, not by any genuine theological dispute.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Joab and Abner meet at the pool of Gibeon. A brutal twelve-on-twelve combat tournament leads to a full battle. Asahel pursues Abner, refuses to turn aside, and is killed. The narrator shows the fratricidal tragedy of civil war: Israelites killing Israelites, both sides burying their dead.
verseByVerse.theology: Abner's killing of Asahel — reluctant, warned, finally necessary — is one of the chapter's moral complexities. He did not want to kill Joab's brother; he warned him twice to turn aside. But Asahel's refusal to hear counsel produced his own death. The chapter preserves the tragedy without assigning all the fault to one side.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The twelve-on-twelve combat at the pool of Gibeon — apparently a tournament meant to settle the conflict without full battle — degenerates into a general engagement when all twenty-four contestants kill each other simultaneously. Human attempts to limit the cost of conflict often fail spectacularly. Now: Civil war in the body of Christ — whether ecclesiastical division, denominational conflict, or interpersonal fracture — always costs more than the participants expect and harms people who had no part in starting it.

verseByVerse.quote: Abner the son of Ner, and the servants of Ish-bosheth the son of Saul, went out from Mahanaim to Gibeon. And Joab the son of Zeruiah and the servants of David went out and met them at the pool of Gibeon. And they sat down, the one on the one side of the pool, and the other on the other side of the pool. And Abner said to Joab, 'Let the young men arise and compete before us.' And Joab said, 'Let them arise.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The pool of Gibeon — a large circular cistern cut from rock, discovered archaeologically in the 1950s — becomes the setting for one of the most vivid scenes in the book. Two armies, both Israelite, face each other across a pool. Abner proposes a tournament — twelve versus twelve — apparently hoping to decide the conflict through representative combat rather than full battle. The proposal has the quality of two generals who both know the war is ultimately unwinnable and are looking for a way to limit the damage.

The result is catastrophic: all twenty-four die simultaneously, each seizing his opponent's head and driving his sword into his side. The site is named Helkath-hazzurim — Field of Sword-Edges, or Field of the Adversaries. Far from limiting the conflict, the tournament ignites a full battle. Alistair Begg notes that this scene is a parable of every attempt to manage the consequences of rebellion against God's order through human ingenuity: the tournament that was meant to save lives costs twenty-four in its first act and triggers a battle that costs many more. The only solution to the civil war is the one that eventually comes — Abner's defection and Ish-bosheth's collapse — not a tactical workaround.

verseByVerse.quote: And Abner said to Asahel, 'Turn aside from following me. Why should I strike you to the ground? How then could I lift up my face to your brother Joab?' But he refused to turn aside. Therefore Abner struck him in the stomach with the butt of his spear, so that the spear came out at his back. And he fell there and died where he was.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Asahel's pursuit of Abner is one of the chapter's most poignant episodes. He is fast as a gazelle, relentless, fixed on the target of the opposing general. Abner twice warns him to turn aside — Turn aside from following me. Why should I strike you to the ground? — not from cowardice but from a genuine reluctance to kill a young man he knows will create a blood-feud with Joab. But Asahel will not turn aside, and Abner kills him with the butt of his spear in an act of lethal self-defense.

The killing of Asahel is the seed of Joab's eventual murder of Abner (3:27), which Joab will justify as blood vengeance. The narrator records the warning Abner gave, making clear that the death was unnecessary on Asahel's part — he chose his fate by refusing counsel. This is not to excuse Abner or minimize the loss; it is to show the complex moral weave of civil war, where the same act can be simultaneously understandable, tragic, and productive of further violence. The grief of the civil war chapters is that everyone is, to some degree, a victim of a situation created by a few. David weeps over Abner's death (3:33–34); he has no pleasure in any of this. The throne he is ascending is being built on sorrow he did not choose and cannot fully prevent.

2.theology: The Kingdom That Comes Through Inquiry. David's opening act — inquiring of the LORD before moving — establishes the governing principle of his best years and the implicit contrast with every subsequent failure. The Bathsheba chapter (11) begins not with an inquiry but with a passive decision to stay home when kings go out to battle. The pattern of seeking God's direction is not merely a spiritual discipline; it is the structural principle on which the Davidic kingdom is built. Where it holds, the kingdom advances; where it breaks down, the consequences are catastrophic.
2.examples:
Then: The seven-year civil war at the start of 2 Samuel is one of the costliest periods of the Davidic story — not because David was wrong but because the human resistance to God's appointed order is always costly to those caught in it. The kingdom of God comes; the question is whether it comes easily or through prolonged conflict driven by human ambition.

Now: The chapter speaks to anyone in a transitional season — between the private calling and the public confirmation, between the anointing and the coronation. David spent seven years in Hebron, honored as king of one tribe, while God's full purpose worked itself out. The wisdom is to do what David did: inquire, obey the specific directive, extend grace where you can, and trust God's timing for the rest.

3.title: Abner's Defection and Joab's Revenge
3.text: <sup>9</sup>'May God do so to Abner and more also, if I do not accomplish for David what the LORD has sworn to him, to transfer the kingdom from the house of Saul and set up the throne of David over Israel and over Judah, from Dan to Beersheba.' <sup>33</sup>And the king lamented for Abner, saying, 'Should Abner die as a fool dies? Your hands were not bound; your feet were not fettered.' (ESV)
3.overview:
Chapter 3 marks the beginning of the end for the house of Saul. Abner, who has been the real power behind Ish-bosheth's throne, breaks with the king over a dispute about Saul's concubine — a dispute that functions as a challenge to Abner's own succession plans. In his anger, he opens negotiations with David, invoking the LORD's own sworn promise to transfer the kingdom to David. He is not a convert to David's cause; he is a calculating general who has decided that alignment with the winning side is now in his interest. But God uses even self-interested defections to accomplish his purposes.

Abner's death at Joab's hand is one of the chapter's central moral problems. Joab kills him at the city gate of Hebron — a place of legal sanctuary — in an act of blood vengeance for Asahel's death, but also (the narrator implies) from fear that Abner's defection will displace Joab's position in David's army. David's response — public mourning, the lament over Abner, the declaration of his own innocence, the curse on Joab's house — shows both his genuine grief and his political constraints: he is not yet strong enough to punish his most powerful general. The chapter ends with the house of Saul growing weaker and the house of David growing stronger, but the cost has been high.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–11 — Abner's Growing Power and the Quarrel
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The war drags on with David's house gaining and Saul's house weakening. David's growing family at Hebron is listed. Ish-bosheth accuses Abner of sleeping with Saul's concubine — a political challenge Abner refuses to accept, and his furious oath opens the door to David's kingdom.
verseByVerse.theology: Abner's oath — invoking God's sworn promise to David — is theologically remarkable: the enemy general acknowledges the divine verdict even while he has been fighting against it. Sometimes God's purposes are advanced by those who finally acknowledge what they have been resisting. The truth of God's promise does not depend on the motives of those who eventually concede it.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Taking a king's concubine was tantamount to claiming the throne (cf. Absalom taking David's concubines in ch. 16; Adonijah asking for Abishag in 1 Kings 2). Abner knew what the accusation implied, and his rage was proportionate to the threat to his own position. Now: Quarrels about succession and power within institutions that belong to God are never merely political — they always have a theological dimension, and they almost always cost more than they needed to.

verseByVerse.quote: There was a long war between the house of Saul and the house of David. And David grew stronger and stronger, while the house of Saul became weaker and weaker. And sons were born to David at Hebron... These were born to David in Hebron.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The narrator inserts a list of David's sons born at Hebron — six sons by six wives — between the war summary and the chapter's central drama. The list serves multiple purposes: it establishes that David's house is growing, not just militarily but dynastically; it introduces the names (Amnon, Absalom, Adonijah) that will cause enormous grief in later chapters; and it demonstrates that the polygamy Israel's kings were warned against in Deuteronomy 17:17 was already taking root in David's household. The seeds of future disaster are planted in the list of births that marks a season of triumph.

The war summary — David grew stronger and stronger, while the house of Saul became weaker and weaker — is the narrator's compressed verdict on the seven-year civil war. It is not a dramatic reversal but a gradual, inexorable shift in the balance of power, driven ultimately by the divine promise that has been operative since 1 Samuel 16. God does not always work by dramatic intervention; he sometimes works by the slow, steady accumulation of evidence that his word will be fulfilled.

verseByVerse.quote: Now Abner was making himself strong in the house of Saul. And Ish-bosheth said to Abner, 'Why have you gone in to my father's concubine?' Then Abner was very angry over the words of Ish-bosheth and said, 'Am I a dog's head of Judah? To this day I keep showing steadfast love to the house of Saul your father... And now you charge me today with a fault concerning a woman. God do so to Abner and more also, if I do not accomplish for David what the LORD has sworn to him, to transfer the kingdom from the house of Saul and set up the throne of David over Israel and over Judah, from Dan to Beersheba.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Ish-bosheth's accusation — that Abner has been sleeping with Rizpah, Saul's concubine — is either a genuine complaint or a political probe. Either way, it is suicidal: Abner has been the entire military and political infrastructure of his kingdom, and Ish-bosheth has just insulted him in the most damaging way possible. Abner's fury is not primarily moral outrage; it is the rage of a kingmaker who has been treated as a subordinate when he considers himself the power behind the throne.

His oath is the theological hinge of the chapter: God do so to Abner and more also, if I do not accomplish for David what the LORD has sworn to him. In his anger, Abner speaks the truth he has known all along: the LORD has sworn to transfer the kingdom to David. He has been fighting against a divine decree, and now his own fury at Ish-bosheth gives him both the motivation and the theological cover to do what the evidence has always demanded. Sinclair Ferguson observes that God sometimes uses the anger of self-interested people to accomplish his sovereign purposes — Abner is not acting from faith or theological conversion, but the outcome he announces is precisely what God has decreed. The LORD's word will be accomplished even through the vehicles of human ambition and wounded pride.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 22–39 — Joab's Murder and David's Lament
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Joab returns from a raid, learns that Abner was in Hebron and has been let go, and secretly recalls him. He kills Abner at the city gate — in blood vengeance for Asahel but also, the narrator implies, from fear of displacement. David mourns publicly and curses Joab's house.
verseByVerse.theology: Joab's murder of Abner at the city gate — a place of legal sanctuary — is an act of premeditated treachery that violates both covenant law and David's political treaty. David's response (mourning, lament, public declaration of innocence) is the only available response to a general whose military necessity exceeds his accountability for the moment. The reality that the wicked sometimes prosper within the structures of the godly is one of 2 Samuel's most honest teachings.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: David's curse on Joab's house (v. 29) was a genuine declaration of divine justice deferred — Solomon eventually executes it (1 Kings 2:34). The wicked are not always punished immediately, but deferred judgment is not canceled judgment. Now: The leader who cannot yet hold the powerful accountable bears the grief of that constraint, as David does here — but must still name what is true and trust the ultimate justice to God.

verseByVerse.quote: Just then the servants of David arrived with Joab from a raid, bringing much spoil with them. But Abner was not with David at Hebron, for he had sent him away, and he had gone in peace. When Joab came in, they told him, Abner the son of Ner came to the king, and he sent him away, and he has gone in peace.
verseByVerse.commentary: The collision between David's diplomacy and Joab's agenda is set up with quiet narrative precision. Joab returns from a raid to find Abner has been received, blessed, and dismissed in peace - and he cannot accept it. His objection to David frames Abner as a spy, but the narrator gives no indication this is true. It is the language of a man with another motive entirely: Abner killed Joab's brother Asahel (2:23), and Joab has not forgotten. The political conversation with the king is a pretext. Joab intends blood vengeance, and he will exercise it by exploiting David's hospitality and the safe-passage David has just extended. This is the dark underside of the early kingdom: the king's general is not under the king's control. Kidner notes that David's inability to restrain Joab - a pattern that recurs throughout his reign - is one of the great tragic threads of the Samuel narrative.

verseByVerse.quote: When Joab came out from David's presence, he sent messengers after Abner, and they brought him back from the well of Sirah. But David did not know about it. And when Abner returned to Hebron, Joab took him aside into the midst of the gate to speak with him privately, and there he struck him in the stomach, so that he died, for the blood of Asahel his brother.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Joab's murder of Abner is a masterpiece of calculated treachery. He uses a private word — the gesture of a conversation, the expectation of safety at the city gate — as the means of assassination. The city gate in ancient Israel was the place of justice, of legal transaction, of covenant security; to kill there was to violate the most protected space in the city's social order. And Joab does it with a specific irony: he uses the same stomach wound that Abner used to kill Asahel — the butt of the spear through the stomach.

The narrator carefully adds: for the blood of Asahel his brother. This is the blood-vengeance claim — technically legitimate under ancient Near Eastern custom, though Abner had warned Asahel twice and killed him in self-defense. But the timing, the location, and the secrecy all suggest that Joab's motivations were not purely juridical. He has also just learned that Abner was in Hebron negotiating his own potential replacement as David's general. R. C. Sproul notes that Joab is one of the morally complex characters of the entire Bible — genuinely capable, fiercely loyal to David in his own way, and capable of calculated murder when his interests demand it. He is the prototype of the indispensable subordinate who is too dangerous to keep and too powerful to remove.

verseByVerse.quote: And the king lamented for Abner, saying, 'Should Abner die as a fool dies? Your hands were not bound; your feet were not fettered; as one falls before the wicked you have fallen.' And all the people wept again over him. Then all the people came to persuade David to eat bread while it was still day. But David swore, saying, 'God do so to me and more also, if I taste bread or anything else till the sun goes down!' And all the people noticed it, and it pleased them, as everything the king did pleased all the people.
verseByVerse.commentary:
David's lament for Abner is shorter than his lament for Saul and Jonathan, but equally genuine. The question — Should Abner die as a fool dies? — is a protest against the manner of his death: Abner did not die in battle, with warrior's honor; he was assassinated at the gate by a man who pretended to offer him private counsel. His hands were not bound, his feet not fettered — he was not taken by enemies in battle but by treachery in peacetime. The lament is a declaration of injustice: this death is wrong.

David's fast until sundown and his public mourning are politically astute but also genuinely felt. He is furious with Joab — the curse in verse 29 is one of the most comprehensive curses in the OT — and he is publicly separating himself from the murder. His declaration of innocence (I and my kingdom are forever guiltless before the LORD for the blood of Abner the son of Ner) is both legal and theological: he is placing the guilt where it belongs and calling God as witness. And the people's response — it pleased them, as everything the king did pleased all the people — shows that David's public mourning is accomplishing what it needs to accomplish: demonstrating that the king of Israel is not a man who murders his rivals but a man who mourns them. His kingdom is being built on genuine covenant loyalty, not on ruthlessness — however much the ruthless sometimes serve within it.

3.theology: The Kingdom Built Despite Its Servants. Chapter 3 introduces a recurring theme of 2 Samuel: God's purposes advance despite, and sometimes through, the morally compromised actions of David's own followers. Joab is the most prominent example — loyal to David, capable in battle, and willing to commit murder when it suits him. David cannot fully control him; he can only mourn, curse, and wait for the justice God will eventually provide. The kingdom of God is never built by perfect people through clean means; it is built by God through imperfect instruments, and the moral complexity of the building is part of its honest testimony.
3.examples:
Then: The house of Saul weakens; the house of David strengthens. Seven years of civil war, two assassinations, one lament — and the trajectory is unchanged. God's purposes move forward at their own pace, regardless of the obstacles human ambition and violence place in the way.

Now: The chapter speaks to leaders who have discovered that the people working within their organizations are not always operating by the leader's values. David could not prevent Joab's murder of Abner; he could only publicly dissociate himself from it and trust that God would hold Joab accountable in his own time. The responsibility of a leader who cannot yet act is to name what is true, mourn what is wrong, and trust the divine justice that is not limited by the leader's political constraints.

4.title: Ish-bosheth Murdered
4.text: <sup>11</sup>'How much more, when wicked men have killed a righteous man in his own house on his bed, shall I not now require his blood at your hand and destroy you from the earth?' <sup>12</sup>And David commanded his young men, and they killed them and cut off their hands and their feet and hanged them beside the pool at Hebron. But they took the head of Ish-bosheth and buried it in the tomb of Abner at Hebron. (ESV)
4.overview:
Chapter 4 brings the house of Saul to its inglorious end. Two of Ish-bosheth's own captains — Baanah and Rechab, sons of Rimmon — assassinate him in his bed at midday while he is taking a nap. They bring his severed head to David at Hebron, expecting the same reward the Amalekite expected for announcing Saul's death. They receive the same response: execution. The king who has refused to benefit from the murder of his enemies is consistent across every instance.

The chapter's brevity is itself a commentary: the house of Saul ends not with a great battle or a theological verdict but with a nap and two treacherous captains. Ish-bosheth, never a real king, dies as he lived — weakly, without agency, a cipher whose death merely formalizes what had been true since Abner defected. And David's response — executing the murderers, burying the head honorably — demonstrates once again that his kingdom is not built on the assassination of rivals but on the patient accumulation of God's own purposes.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–12 — The End of the House of Saul
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: With Abner dead, Ish-bosheth's hands hang limp (the text's striking image of helplessness). Two of his captains kill him in his sleep, bring his head to David expecting reward. David executes them, buries the head, and the house of Saul ends.
verseByVerse.theology: David's principle — the LORD's anointed is inviolable, and those who claim to serve David by killing his enemies will be held accountable — is applied for the third time (the Amalekite, Abner, Ish-bosheth). The consistency of the principle across three different cases and three different circumstances is the moral testimony of the chapter: David's restraint was not situational but covenantal.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Baanah and Rechab miscalculated David in exactly the same way the Amalekite did — they assumed he would be grateful for the removal of a rival. The assumption that the godly leader shares the ruthlessness of those who serve him is always a miscalculation. Now: Leaders who build their organizations on the willingness of subordinates to do the morally questionable 'for the good of the cause' will eventually discover that the same subordinates will do the same to them.

verseByVerse.quote: When Ish-bosheth, Saul's son, heard that Abner had died at Hebron, his courage failed, and all Israel was dismayed. Now Saul's son had two men who were captains of raiding bands; the name of the one was Baanah, and the name of the other Rechab, the sons of Rimmon a man of Benjamin... They came into the midst of the house as if to get wheat, and they stabbed him in the stomach. Then Rechab and Baanah his brother escaped.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Ish-bosheth's reaction to Abner's death — his courage failed, literally 'his hands became limp' — is the physical image of a man who knows his support structure has been removed. He was never a real king; Abner was always the reality behind the throne. Without Abner, he is simply waiting for the end. The final detail — he is napping in his bed at midday when his own captains kill him — captures the passivity of his entire reign. He does nothing; he waits; things happen to him.

Baanah and Rechab's ruse — entering the house 'as if to get wheat' — is the cover of mundane necessity used to conceal political murder. The image of assassins entering through the kitchen while the king sleeps is almost theatrical in its domestic horror. The head they sever and carry to Hebron is the final trophy of a war they did not fight but think they have ended. Their calculation about David is the same fatal miscalculation of the Amalekite: they have identified what David wants (the throne of all Israel) without understanding how he has determined to get it.

verseByVerse.quote: They brought the head of Ish-bosheth to David at Hebron and said to the king, 'Here is the head of Ish-bosheth, the son of Saul, your enemy, who sought your life. The LORD has avenged my lord the king this day on Saul and on his offspring.' David answered Rechab and Baanah his brother, the sons of Rimmon the Beerothite, 'As the LORD lives, who has redeemed my life out of every adversity, when one told me, Saul is dead, and thought he was bringing good news, I seized him and killed him at Ziklag...'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The argument Baanah and Rechab make — the LORD has avenged my lord the king this day — is theologically rich but practically disastrous. They are right that God is the one who removes Saul's house; they are catastrophically wrong to think they are God's instruments in doing so. The LORD had not commissioned them; they had acted from self-interest and opportunity. Invoking divine purpose to justify unsanctioned action is a recurring human error — and it is rarely received well by those who actually live in dependence on God's direction.

David's response draws the explicit parallel to the Amalekite: the man who told him about Saul's death thought he was bringing good news — and was executed. How much more these men who murdered a sleeping, defenseless man in his own bed? The rhetorical argument (how much more) is the argument from lesser to greater: if the Amalekite was executed for killing a man who was already dying on a battlefield, what punishment is appropriate for premeditated assassination in a private home? David's consistency across all three cases is both a personal integrity statement and a public one: Israel's king will not tolerate murder, even murder of his enemies, even murder done in his name. Alistair Begg notes that the execution of Baanah and Rechab — the severing of their hands and feet, the hanging of their bodies at Hebron — is deliberately visible: it is a public declaration of David's standards, enacted before all Israel as the kingdom of all Israel is about to be offered to him.

4.theology:
The Kingdom Not Built by Murder. Chapters 1–4 form a theological unit around a single principle: David does not advance his kingdom through the deaths of his rivals or enemies, even when those deaths are offered to him on a plate. Three times the pattern repeats: the Amalekite, Joab's murder of Abner, Baanah and Rechab's murder of Ish-bosheth. Each time David responds with grief, execution of the perpetrators, and a public statement of his own innocence. The kingdom of God cannot be built by human ruthlessness — it must be built by God's methods on God's timing.

This principle finds its ultimate expression in the cross. Jesus, who had more legitimate claim to the throne of the universe than David had to the throne of Israel, refused to seize it by force or by the death of his enemies. He waited for the Father's timing, followed the Father's method, and received the kingdom through suffering rather than through violence. David's chapters 1–4 are a thumbnail sketch of Philippians 2:5–11.
4.examples:
Then: The burial of Ish-bosheth's head in the tomb of Abner at Hebron is a final act of covenantal respect: even the man whose kingdom opposed David's received honorable burial at David's command. The enemy dead are honored; the murderers are executed. This is the kingdom's moral order.

Now: The chapter challenges the contemporary instinct to justify ethically questionable means by appealing to good ends — 'the LORD wants this outcome, therefore this action serves him.' David refuses this logic consistently. The ends do not sanctify the means; the LORD's purposes do not require human treachery to accomplish them. Those who volunteer to be God's hit men without divine commission will discover, with Baanah and Rechab, that they have profoundly misread the God they thought they were serving.

5.title: King of All Israel
5.text: <sup>3</sup>So all the elders of Israel came to the king at Hebron, and King David made a covenant with them at Hebron before the LORD, and they anointed David king over Israel. <sup>12</sup>And David knew that the LORD had established him king over Israel, and that he had exalted his kingdom for the sake of his people Israel. (ESV)
5.overview:
Chapter 5 is the coronation chapter — the moment the book has been building toward since 1 Samuel 16, when a shepherd boy in Bethlehem was anointed king in the sight of his brothers. Now, after fourteen years of exile, fugitive wandering, civil war, and patient waiting, David is anointed king over all Israel at Hebron. The chapter does not celebrate with extended rhetoric; it records the fact with characteristic narrative brevity and immediately moves to the challenges the new kingdom faces: the capture of Jerusalem, the building of the palace, the Philistine response.

The theological key of the chapter is verse 12: David knew that the LORD had established him king over Israel, and that he had exalted his kingdom for the sake of his people Israel. This is the interpretive principle for everything that follows in the chapter. David's military successes — Jerusalem taken, the Philistines twice defeated — are not evidence of his own military genius but of the LORD's faithfulness to his promise. The kingdom belongs to the people, not to the king; the king is the instrument of God's covenant commitment to Israel. This is the theology that, when David forgets it in chapter 11, produces the greatest disaster of his reign.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: All Israel comes to David at Hebron with a covenantal argument: we are your bone and flesh; you were always the real commander of Israel's armies; the LORD has already designated you. The covenant is made; the anointing is performed. David is king over all Israel at thirty years old.
verseByVerse.theology: The elders' appeal — bone and flesh — is the covenant formula of kinship and solidarity (cf. Gen. 2:23). They are not merely acknowledging political reality; they are invoking the covenant bonds that make Israel one people. David's kingship is covenantal before it is political.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The seven-year delay between the Judah anointing and the all-Israel anointing was not a failure of God's promise but its careful, providential fulfillment. The waiting period formed both David and the nation. Now: God's confirmations often come in stages — private calling, partial fulfillment, full confirmation — and each stage has its own purpose and its own formation.

verseByVerse.quote: Then all the tribes of Israel came to David at Hebron and said, 'Behold, we are your bone and flesh. In times past, when Saul was king over us, it was you who led out and brought in Israel. And the LORD said to you, You shall be shepherd of my people Israel, and you shall be prince over Israel.' So all the elders of Israel came to the king at Hebron... and they anointed David king over Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The elders of Israel arrive with a triple argument: kinship (we are your bone and flesh), track record (it was you who led out and brought in Israel), and divine mandate (the LORD said to you...). Each argument is true. The bone-and-flesh formula echoes the garden — the primal covenant of belonging — applied now to a political covenant. The military track record is unimpeachable: even under Saul's jealous management, it was David who won the battles. And the divine mandate is the one that David has waited longest to see acknowledged by those who opposed it.

The title the elders use — shepherd of my people Israel — is both pastoral and royal, and it links David to the great shepherd-kings of the ancient world and to the God who is Israel's own shepherd (Psalm 23). John 10's portrait of Jesus as the Good Shepherd is drawing from this deep well: the king who is also a shepherd, who knows his sheep by name, who leads them out and brings them in. David's title at his coronation is the title that will find its definitive fulfillment in the Son of David who lays down his life for his flock.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: David captures the Jebusite stronghold of Jerusalem — so impregnable that its defenders mock him with the blind and the lame — and makes it his capital. He builds there; Hiram of Tyre sends materials and craftsmen; David's household grows. The theological key: David knew the LORD had established him for the sake of his people.
verseByVerse.theology: Jerusalem's capture is a divine gift, not merely a military conquest. The Jebusites' confidence in their fortress echoes the confidence of every human stronghold that has not reckoned with the living God. The city David captures will become the city of God's own dwelling — the site of the temple, the place where heaven meets earth, the city toward which all of Scripture ultimately moves.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Jebusites' taunt — even the blind and lame can defend against you — was the kind of contempt that only invites defeat by a God who delights to confound human confidence. Now: The strongholds that seem most impregnable to the gospel are sometimes the first to fall when God moves.

verseByVerse.quote: And the king and his men went to Jerusalem against the Jebusites... And the Jebusites said to David, 'You will not come in here, but the blind and the lame will ward you off' — thinking, 'David cannot come in here.' Nevertheless, David took the stronghold of Zion, that is, the city of David... And David knew that the LORD had established him king over Israel, and that he had exalted his kingdom for the sake of his people Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The choice of Jerusalem as capital is theologically as well as militarily brilliant. It belongs to no tribe — it is not Benjaminite territory (Saul's tribe) or Judahite territory (David's tribe) — which makes it a neutral capital for a newly united kingdom. And its capture from the Jebusites, who have held it since before the conquest, is a demonstration that the divine mandate given to Joshua centuries earlier has not expired. The land promise and the kingship promise are being fulfilled together.

The Jebusites' taunt — even the blind and the lame will ward you off — may be a reference to sacred objects or guardian figures at the entrance to their stronghold; whatever its precise meaning, it expresses complete contempt for David's military capacity. They are wrong. The city falls. And David's response to the capture is not a monument to his own generalship but a theological statement: David knew that the LORD had established him king. The victory belongs to God; the city belongs to the LORD. Every achievement of David's reign that is read through this lens will be understood correctly; every achievement he reads through the lens of his own power will lead him astray. R. C. Sproul writes that verse 12 is the interpretive key to the entire chapter, and arguably to the entire Davidic kingship: the throne exists for the sake of God's people, not for the sake of the king.

verseByVerse.quote: And David took more concubines and wives from Jerusalem, after he came from Hebron, and more sons and daughters were born to David.
verseByVerse.commentary: The terse listing of David's expanding household sits awkwardly in the narrative's triumphant arc - and the discomfort is intentional. Deuteronomy 17:17 warned the king explicitly: he shall not acquire many wives for himself, lest his heart turn away. The narrator records this accumulation without editorial comment, but the reader who knows the law hears the warning bell. The names of the children born in Jerusalem include Solomon - the son through whom the Davidic covenant will run - but the same household contains the seeds of Absalom's rebellion (cf. chs. 13-19). Waltke notes that the Bible's realism here is a form of pastoral honesty: God works through David despite David, not because David is flawless. The triumph of Jerusalem cannot erase the shadow that polygamy casts over the house of David from this point forward.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: When the Philistines hear David has been anointed king of all Israel, they mobilize against him. David inquires of the LORD twice — once receiving a direct command to attack, once receiving a specific battle strategy of flanking through the balsam trees. Both battles are won as God directs.
verseByVerse.theology: The two battles show a consistent pattern: David asks, God answers specifically, David obeys exactly, the victory comes. The strategy of the second battle — attack when you hear the sound of marching in the tops of the balsam trees — is a divine military directive that makes no natural sense but produces victory. Obedience to specific, seemingly unusual divine instruction is the mark of faith.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Philistines mobilized at Rephaim — the same valley below Jerusalem, familiar from Goliath's campaign. But this time Israel has a king who asks God rather than trembling in tents. Now: The same challenge faced differently because the same person is living differently — not from changed circumstances but from changed dependence — is one of the most common patterns of spiritual growth.

verseByVerse.quote: And David inquired of the LORD, 'Shall I go up against the Philistines? Will you give them into my hand?' And the LORD said to David, 'Go up, for I will certainly give the Philistines into your hand.'... And he came to Baal-perazim, and David defeated them there. And David said, 'The LORD has broken through my enemies before me like a breaking flood.' Therefore the name of that place is called Baal-perazim.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The name David gives to the site of the first victory — Baal-perazim, 'the LORD of breaking through' — is a theological declaration compressed into a place-name. The LORD has broken through the Philistines like a flood breaking through a dam. The image is not of careful military strategy but of irresistible divine force: the enemies are not defeated so much as swept away. David does not name the place after his own generalship; he names it after the God who made the breakthrough possible.

The second battle's strategy — wait until you hear the sound of marching in the tops of the balsam trees — is one of the most intriguing divine directives in the OT. The sound in the treetops may be a theophanic presence, a divine army moving through the trees to strike the Philistines from behind. Whatever its precise nature, it requires David to subordinate his military instincts to a specific divine signal: do not attack until you hear that sound, then attack quickly, because the LORD has gone before you. Alistair Begg notes that the second battle's strategy would make no sense to a military planner working from natural principles alone — it requires the kind of trust that only comes from a consistent pattern of inquiry and obedience. David's military genius is not the content of the strategy; it is the willingness to follow the strategy God gives rather than the one he would devise himself.

5.theology: The Kingdom Established for the People's Sake. Verse 12's summary — the LORD had established David king for the sake of his people — is the theological principle that governs all legitimate authority in God's economy. Authority is not self-referential; it exists for the welfare of those under it. The king who forgets this and uses the kingdom for himself has already begun the decline that chapters 11–20 will document. Every legitimate authority in human society — civil, ecclesiastical, familial — exists to serve those under it, not to consume them. David's best years are the years when he holds this principle clearly; his worst years are when he loses it.
5.examples:
Then: David's capture of Jerusalem as a neutral capital — belonging to no tribe, newly taken from pagans, strategically central — was a moment of political genius grounded in theological purpose. The city he takes becomes the city of God, the place of the temple, the eschatological center of all human history. He builds better than he knows.

Now: The chapter speaks to every person in a season of confirmed calling who discovers that the confirmation brings new challenges rather than rest. David is anointed king over all Israel and immediately faces Jerusalem, then the Philistines. Confirmation of God's purposes does not eliminate opposition; it often intensifies it. The answer is the same in the new chapter as in the old: inquire of the LORD before you act, and follow what he gives precisely.

6.title: The Ark Comes to Jerusalem
6.text: <sup>14</sup>And David danced before the LORD with all his might. And David was wearing a linen ephod. <sup>16</sup>As the ark of the LORD came into the city of David, Michal the daughter of Saul looked out of the window and saw King David leaping and dancing before the LORD, and she despised him in her heart. (ESV)
6.overview:
Chapter 6 is the ark chapter — one of the most theologically rich and emotionally intense chapters in the book. David's desire to bring the ark to Jerusalem is genuine and God-honoring: he wants the symbol of God's presence at the center of his new capital, the covenant dwelling of the LORD among his people. But the first attempt goes wrong spectacularly: Uzzah reaches out to steady the ark and dies. David is angry, then afraid, then humbled. He spends three months learning what the first attempt failed to ask: how does God want to be approached?

The second attempt succeeds — with dancing, sacrifice, celebration, and the ark installed in its tent. And then: Michal. She despises David's undignified worship, and their confrontation at the chapter's end is one of the most revealing dialogues in the book. David's response — I will celebrate before the LORD. I will become even more undignified than this — is both a defense of authentic worship and a declaration of who his audience is. His worship is directed to God, not to the watching court. Michal's contempt is the contempt of religious decorum for genuine devotion, and the judgment on her — childless to the day of her death — is as solemn as anything in the chapter.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–11 — Uzzah's Death and David's Fear
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: David assembles thirty thousand men to bring the ark to Jerusalem. They transport it on a cart — the Philistine method, not God's prescribed method. At the threshing floor of Nacon, the oxen stumble and Uzzah reaches out to steady the ark. He dies immediately. David is angry, then afraid. He leaves the ark at Obed-edom's house for three months.
verseByVerse.theology: Uzzah's death is the most shocking moment of the chapter and one of the most difficult in the entire OT. But its logic is the logic of Levitical holiness: the ark was to be carried by Levites on poles (Num. 4:15; 7:9), not transported on a cart. Uzzah's death was not arbitrary cruelty but the consequence of casual handling of the holy — the same lesson Beth-shemesh learned in 1 Samuel 6. The God who is approached wrongly becomes a consuming fire.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Philistines had transported the ark on a cart (1 Sam. 6) — it was their method, not Israel's. David copied the pagan method of transporting the most sacred object in Israel, and the result was catastrophic. Adopting the world's methods for handling sacred things tends to produce the same result. Now: The lesson is not that God kills people for minor liturgical errors; it is that the manner in which we approach God matters — not as performance but as acknowledgment of who he is.

verseByVerse.quote: David again gathered all the chosen men of Israel, thirty thousand. And David arose and went with all the people who were with him from Baale-judah to bring up from there the ark of God... And they carried the ark of God on a new cart and brought it out of the house of Abinadab, which was on the hill. And Uzzah and Ahio, the sons of Abinadab, were driving the new cart... And Uzzah put out his hand to the ark of God and took hold of it, for the oxen stumbled. And the anger of the LORD was kindled against Uzzah, and God struck him down there because of his error, and he died there beside the ark of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The energy of the procession is enormous — thirty thousand people, music, dancing, celebration. David is doing something genuinely good: he wants the ark at the center of his new capital, the presence of God at the heart of the nation's life. But the method is wrong. The Levitical law specified that the ark was to be carried on poles by specific Kohathite Levites (Num. 4:15); the cart method was the Philistines' improvisation (1 Sam. 6:7–8), adopted without checking what God had actually commanded. The magnificent new cart is, in God's economy, precisely the wrong approach.

When the oxen stumble and Uzzah reaches out to steady the ark, the instinct seems natural — even admirable. He is trying to prevent the sacred object from falling to the ground. But the law was explicit: even the Kohathites who were authorized to carry it were not to touch it directly (Num. 4:15), and Uzzah is not a Kohathite. His death is the enforcement of a holiness boundary that Israel had been treating as optional. R. C. Sproul writes that Uzzah's death forces the question every person must eventually face: on whose terms is God to be approached? Not ours. Not the terms we improvise from good intentions and borrowed pagan methods. His terms, revealed in his word, followed precisely. The God who is not approached on his own terms becomes dangerous, not because he is capricious but because holiness and casual handling are permanently incompatible.

verseByVerse.quote: And David was angry because the LORD had broken out against Uzzah. And that place is called Perez-uzzah to this day. And David was afraid of the LORD that day, and he said, 'How can the ark of the LORD come to me?' And David was not willing to take the ark of the LORD into the city of David. But David took it aside to the house of Obed-edom the Gittite. And the ark of the LORD remained in the house of Obed-edom the Gittite three months, and the LORD blessed Obed-edom and all his household.
verseByVerse.commentary:
David's anger is honest and troubling — he is angry at God for what feels like disproportionate punishment of a man whose instinct was to protect the ark. This is not the right response, but it is a real one, and the narrator records it without smoothing it over. The anger gives way to fear: How can the ark of the LORD come to me? The same question Beth-shemesh asked after the seventy died (1 Sam. 6:20). Who can stand before this holy God? The fear is the right response; it leads to inquiry and correction.

The three months the ark spends at Obed-edom's house are a grace period — both for David to learn the correct method (1 Chron. 15:13 makes explicit that David did his research during this period: we did not seek him according to the rule) and a demonstration of what happens when the ark is handled rightly: the LORD blessed Obed-edom and all his household. The God who is deadly to the careless is life-giving to the reverent. The same holiness that killed Uzzah blessed Obed-edom. Holiness is not simply dangerous; it is dangerous to casual handling and gracious to reverent approach.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12–23 — The Ark Arrives; Michal's Contempt
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: David learns that Obed-edom is blessed and brings the ark up to Jerusalem with proper Levitical transport, sacrifices every six steps, and dances before the LORD with all his might. Michal, watching from a window, despises him. Their confrontation after the celebration reveals the gulf between authentic worship and religious propriety.
verseByVerse.theology: David's dancing before the LORD — in a linen ephod, 'with all his might' — is not performance but self-forgetful devotion. His audience is God, not the court. Michal's contempt is the contempt of social dignity for genuine abandon before God, and the judgment on her measures the gravity of despising authentic worship.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: David's response to Michal — I will become even more undignified than this — is not petulance but principle: worship directed to God cannot be calibrated to the comfort of bystanders. Now: The tension between dignified religious form and authentic personal devotion is present in every generation of the church. The standard is not decorum but genuine self-forgetful encounter with the living God.

verseByVerse.quote: And it was told King David, 'The LORD has blessed the household of Obed-edom and all that belongs to him, because of the ark of God.' So David went and brought up the ark of God from the house of Obed-edom to the city of David with rejoicing. And when those who bore the ark of the LORD had gone six steps, he sacrificed an ox and a fattened animal. And David danced before the LORD with all his might. And David was wearing a linen ephod.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The second procession is a study in contrast to the first. Where the first used a cart, this one uses Levites with poles (1 Chron. 15 supplies the details). Where the first sacrificed nowhere along the route, this one sacrifices every six steps — a rhythm of worship punctuating every small advance of the divine presence. Where the first produced a funeral, this one produces dancing. The method has changed; the outcome changes with it. David wears a linen ephod — the garment of a priest, not a king — deliberately setting aside royal dignity to stand before God in priestly simplicity.

The dancing with all his might — the Hebrew suggests spinning, leaping, an unselfconscious physicality of worship — is one of the most human moments in David's story. He is not performing for the crowd; he is responding to the God who has restored what was lost, who has brought his presence back to Israel, who has blessed Obed-edom and is now blessing Jerusalem. The Psalms David writes are full of this quality — let everything that has breath praise the LORD — and this moment is the living embodiment of that theology. Genuine encounter with the living God produces an abandon that does not ask how it looks to observers.

verseByVerse.quote: As the ark of the LORD came into the city of David, Michal the daughter of Saul looked out of the window and saw King David leaping and dancing before the LORD, and she despised him in her heart... David said to Michal, 'It was before the LORD, who chose me above your father and above all his house, to appoint me as prince over Israel, the people of the LORD — and I will celebrate before the LORD. I will become even more undignified than this, and I will be abased in my own eyes.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Michal's contempt — How the king of Israel honored himself today, uncovering himself today before the eyes of his servants' female servants, as one of the vulgar fellows shamelessly uncovers himself! — is the voice of aristocratic religious propriety confronting genuine devotion. She is not wrong about the facts: David was undignified. She is profoundly wrong about the standard: David's worship was not addressed to the watching court but to the LORD who chose him.

David's response deserves close reading. He begins with theology — it was before the LORD, who chose me above your father — and establishes who his audience was. He then makes the most astonishing declaration: I will become even more undignified than this, and I will be abased in my own eyes. Abasement in his own eyes, exaltation in the eyes of the servant girls — this is the inversion of Hannah's song (2:8), the reversal of human status that is the grammar of all genuine worship. The person who is most concerned with their own dignity before God has not yet understood what they are approaching. Tim Keller writes that genuine worship is always characterized by a loss of self-consciousness before God — not by emotional manipulation but by the natural consequence of actually encountering the holy God, before whom all human pretension falls away.

The judgment on Michal — childless to the day of her death — is solemn and final. It is not a punishment for disagreeing with David; it is the consequence of despising the worship of the LORD. Specifically, she despised David's worship in her heart — the narrator has tracked the internal state from the beginning. The issue is not her words but her heart's orientation toward God's chosen king and God's chosen worship. The barrenness is the mirror of the spiritual emptiness her contempt reflects.

6.theology: Approaching God on His Terms. The chapter's double lesson — Uzzah's death and David's dancing — together address the two failures in worship: approaching God carelessly (as if his holiness doesn't matter) and approaching him with cold propriety (as if his grace doesn't overwhelm). The right approach combines reverence and abandon: the Levites who carry the ark carefully on poles, stopping every six steps for sacrifice; and the king who dances with all his might in priestly simplicity before the God who chose him. Both are required; neither alone is adequate.
6.examples:
Then: The ark's arrival in Jerusalem is the beginning of the theocratic monarchy at its highest expression: the king who is also a worshipper, who dances before the God he serves, who brings the divine presence to the center of the city.
