She appeals to his self-interest (you will be like one of the outrageous fools in Israel), to the possibility of a legitimate solution (please speak to the king, for he will not withhold me from you), and to the consequences for herself (where could I carry my shame?). Her arguments are reasonable, courageous, and entirely ignored. Amnon's lust is not susceptible to reason; R. C. Sproul writes that this is the consistent testimony of scripture about unrestrained desire — it does not hear the counsel of wisdom because it has already decided what it wants. Proverbs' description of the path to the adulteress's house (Prov. 7:7–23) could have been written about Amnon's chapter: a young man void of understanding, walking down a path that leads to death, deaf to every warning.

The assault is described with brutal brevity. And then, immediately afterward: Then Amnon hated her with very great hatred, so that the hatred with which he hated her was greater than the love with which he had loved her. This verse is one of the most psychologically precise in the Bible: the lust that masqueraded as love was instantly unmasked by its fulfillment as contempt. Love that is really lust loves the forbidden object; once the object is possessed, the 'love' evaporates and the displaced self-loathing turns into hatred of the object. Amnon treats Tamar as an object throughout — first of obsession, then of contempt — and never as a person. This is the grammar of all lust: it consumes persons as means to its own satisfaction and discards them when satisfied.

sections.title: Tamar's Desolation and David's Failure
sections.commentary:
Tamar's grief is expressed in the most complete and visible forms available to her: tearing her garment (the long robe of the king's virgin daughters — its tearing signals the violation of the status it represents), putting ashes on her head, crying aloud as she goes. She does not hide her grief; she declares it publicly. And her final destination — Absalom's house, remaining desolate — is the chapter's most desolate fact. Desolate in Hebrew (shomemah) means laid waste, devastated; it is used of destroyed cities and ravaged land. Tamar is the city Amnon has laid waste, and she will remain so.

David's response is the chapter's second moral failure after Amnon's assault: When King David heard of all these things, he was very angry, but he would not punish his son, for he loved him, because he was his firstborn. The parenthetical reason — 'for he loved him, because he was his firstborn' — is the Eli pattern. David knows. He is angry. He does nothing. His anger without action is worse than ignorance, because it demonstrates that he has both the knowledge and the capacity to act and still refuses. The failure to exercise justice for Tamar because of love for Amnon produces the conditions for Absalom's two-year cold rage and eventual murder. Every step of the sword's progress through David's house is traceable to a previous failure to act when action was required.

sections.title: Absalom's Cold Revenge
sections.commentary:
Absalom waits two years. The patience of his planning is itself a kind of horror: he does not act from hot anger but from cold calculation. He invites all the king's sons to his sheep-shearing at Baal-hazor, specifically asking for Amnon, and when Amnon is drunk, has him killed. The murder is an act of justice — Amnon deserved punishment that David failed to administer — executed through an act of treachery at a festival, by servants acting under orders. The justice is real; the method is wrong; the motivation is mixed at best.

Absalom flees to Geshur, his maternal grandfather's kingdom, where he remains for three years. David mourns Amnon — the narrator adds: and the soul of King David longed to go out to Absalom, for he was comforted about Amnon, since he was dead. David grieves his murdered son and simultaneously longs for his murderer son. This is the genuine complexity of parental love in a household destroyed by the consequences of the parent's own sin. He cannot bring Amnon back; he cannot yet bring Absalom home; he sits in Jerusalem with the sword Nathan promised, cutting through his family one blow at a time.

Tim Keller observes that chapter 13 is the clearest evidence that David's sin was not simply a personal moral failure — it was a covenantal and familial one, and its consequences are covenantal and familial. The man who could not govern his own household could not fully govern the nation; the king who refused to discipline himself could not adequately discipline his children. The chapter is the anatomy of multi-generational consequence: sin passes down not by genetic determinism but by the concrete failures of modeling and discipline that shape the next generation's character and choices.

13.theology: The Sword That Does Not Depart. Chapter 13 is the first blow of Nathan's announced sword. It is essential to read it not as a story about Amnon's lust (though it is that) but as the first consequence of David's sin working itself out in his children. The patterns are identical: David saw, desired, and took a woman he had no right to; Amnon sees, desires, and takes a woman he has no right to. David covered his sin by arranging Uriah's death; Absalom covers his grievance by arranging Amnon's death. The sins of the father are reproduced and amplified in the children, not by fate but by the concrete patterns of behavior modeled and the failures of discipline that left the children to their own unrestrained desires.
13.examples:
Then: Tamar's voice — warning, reasoning, pleading, mourning — is the chapter's moral standard. She is the only person in the chapter whose conduct is unimpeachable: she resists what she cannot ultimately prevent, mourns what has been done to her without shame, and grieves honestly. The chapter's injustice is that her voice is the one least heard by the men whose responsibility it was to hear it.

Now: The chapter speaks with pastoral directness to the reality of sexual violence in every era: it names it, shows its consequences, and indicts those in authority who fail to act. The church that is silent about Tamar's experience in its own community is repeating David's failure. And it calls every person to examine the patterns they are modeling for their children — not because children are robots who reproduce the parental template, but because the absence of discipline and the presence of modeled sin create the conditions in which the next generation's choices are formed.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Amnon, David's eldest son, is obsessed with his half-sister Tamar. His cousin Jonadab devises a scheme. Amnon feigns illness, asks for Tamar to cook for him, and then rapes her. Then he despises her. David hears and is furious but does not punish his son. Absalom, Tamar's full brother, takes her in and nurses his hatred for two years.
verseByVerse.theology: The chapter fulfills Nathan's prophecy in chapter 12: the sword will never depart from your house, and I will raise up evil against you from within your own household. The sins of the father echo through the children: David's adultery and murder become Amnon's rape and Absalom's murder. MacArthur notes that David's failure to discipline Amnon - partly because he loved him and partly because his own moral authority had been compromised by his own sin - is the proximate cause of the family's unraveling.
verseByVerse.examples: Ferguson observes that Amnon's hatred of Tamar after the assault is as intense as his desire before it. This is the anatomy of lust: it masquerades as love until it possesses its object, and then it recognizes what it always was. Tamar's desolation - she lived a desolate woman in her brother Absalom's house - is one of the most heartbreaking verses in the Old Testament.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Amnon hated her with very great hatred, so that the hatred with which he hated her was greater than the love with which he had loved her. And Amnon said to her, Get up! Go! But she said to him, No, my brother, for this wrong in sending me away is greater than the other that you did to me.
verseByVerse.commentary: Tamar understands what Amnon does not: under the law, sending her away is in some ways worse than the assault. Her life is ruined either way; at least if he kept her, there would be a legal framework. But he despises her and throws her out. She tears her long robe - the garment of the virgin daughters of the king - puts ashes on her head, and walks away weeping. Absalom sees and understands. He says nothing to Amnon: Absalom hated Amnon because he had violated his sister Tamar. Two years of silence. David does nothing. The silence and inaction of the men in Tamar's life who should have protected her is its own devastating commentary.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: After two years, Absalom arranges a sheep-shearing feast and has his servants kill Amnon. The other princes flee in panic. Absalom flees to his grandfather's house in Geshur and remains there three years. David mourns for Absalom every day.
verseByVerse.theology: Absalom's act is understandable by human justice but belongs to God alone. He has waited two years, arranged it carefully, and executed Amnon. The justice he delivers is real - Amnon deserved punishment - but it was not his to deliver. He becomes, in the act of avenging his sister, another version of the violence he was avenging. Sproul notes that the chain of sin-revenge-further-sin that runs through the house of David is a portrait of what happens when a family loses its moral center.
verseByVerse.examples: Kidner observes that David's daily mourning for Absalom during the three-year exile shows the divided heart that will define David's relationship with his son: he loves him, he mourns for him, but he cannot bring himself either to punish or to fully reconcile. This ambivalence will cost him dearly.

verseByVerse.quote: Absalom fled and went to Geshur, and was there three years. And the spirit of the king longed to go out to Absalom, because he was comforted about Amnon, since he was dead.
verseByVerse.commentary: Absalom's flight to Geshur (his mother's homeland) saves his life and begins a five-year exile from his father's presence. David knows what Absalom has done; he mourns Amnon; but over time the grief for his dead son is replaced by longing for his living one. The sentence David mourned for his son every day (v.37) likely means Absalom, not Amnon. The king who could have prevented all of this by acting justly at the beginning now lives in the grief that his passivity created.

14.title: Joab's Stratagem; Absalom's Return
14.text: <sup>14</sup>'We must all die; we are like water spilled on the ground, which cannot be gathered up again. But God will not take away life, and he devises means so that the banished one will not remain an outcast.' <sup>33</sup>And the king kissed Absalom. (ESV)
14.overview:
Chapter 14 is a chapter about restoration — and about how the wrong kind of restoration creates the conditions for the wrong kind of return. Joab, reading David's yearning for Absalom, engineers a stratagem through a wise woman of Tekoa to persuade David to bring Absalom home. The woman's argument is theologically rich: God devises means so that the banished one will not remain an outcast. David is persuaded to allow Absalom's return — but the return is incomplete. For two years Absalom lives in Jerusalem without seeing the king's face. When he finally forces a meeting through Joab (by burning Joab's barley field), the reconciliation is grudging and partial: a formal kiss that satisfies protocol without restoring relationship.

The problem with the chapter's outcome is not that Absalom returns but that he returns without accountability, without repentance, without genuine reconciliation. Joab engineered the return for political reasons (he wanted Absalom positioned as successor); David permitted it from emotional need rather than covenantal wisdom. The result is an Absalom who is physically present in Jerusalem but spiritually and relationally unreconciled — which is the most dangerous condition in which to leave a proud, ambitious, politically skilled son. Chapter 15's rebellion is the direct result of chapter 14's botched restoration.

sections.title: The Wise Woman's Parable
sections.commentary:
Joab's deployment of the wise woman of Tekoa follows Nathan's model but serves a different purpose. Where Nathan's parable exposed sin, this parable seeks to move David toward a predetermined conclusion. The woman's invented story — two sons fighting, one killing the other, the clan demanding the killer's death — is designed to elicit the same judicial instinct that Nathan engaged: the king's sense of justice applied to a case that mirrors his own, then turned back on him. David grants her request: the avenger of blood shall not destroy her son. And then she reveals the application: why has the king not brought back his own banished son?

Her theological argument — we must all die; we are like water spilled on the ground, which cannot be gathered up again. But God will not take away life, and he devises means so that the banished one will not remain an outcast — is genuine wisdom. The image of spilled water, the acknowledgment that death cannot be undone, the affirmation of God's creative mercy in finding ways to restore the banished — this is genuine OT theology. The problem is not the theology but the application: she is using it to justify the restoration of a murderer without accountability, a restoration Joab wants for political rather than spiritual reasons. True theology can be deployed in the service of false goals. R. C. Sproul notes that the woman's argument is right about God's character but wrong about the specific application — God does devise means for restoration, but those means normally include repentance. The Absalom whom Joab wants restored has shown no repentance whatsoever.

sections.title: The Partial Return and the Full Alienation
sections.commentary:
Absalom returns to Jerusalem — and waits two full years without seeing the king's face. The return is physical without being relational; it satisfies David's longing to have him near without requiring the harder work of genuine reconciliation. This is one of the most psychologically astute observations in the book: Absalom is in the city, at liberty, accumulating grievances, while David refuses both to punish him fully and to restore him fully. The limbo state — neither exile nor full restoration — is the worst possible outcome for a proud and ambitious man.

Absalom's description at this point in the narrative — his beauty, his hair, his children — is the narrator's way of establishing the character we are dealing with: a man of extraordinary personal attractiveness and visible abundance, who is nonetheless burning with resentment at perceived injustice. His burning of Joab's barley field to force a meeting is an act of calculated aggression: he will not tolerate being ignored. When he finally stands before the king and the king kisses him, the reconciliation has been forced rather than sought, engineered rather than genuine. The kiss that ends the chapter is one of the most ambiguous gestures in the book: it satisfies the form of reconciliation without its substance, and it sets in motion the rebellion that chapters 15–20 will document. Sinclair Ferguson writes that David's management of the Absalom situation is a portrait of well-intentioned pastoral failure: he wanted the relationship restored without being willing to pay the cost of the honest conversation that genuine restoration required. The result was a surface peace over a deep wound, and surface peace over deep wounds always eventually explodes.

14.theology: Restoration That Does Not Restore. Chapter 14's central theological problem is the gap between the form of restoration and its reality. David allows Absalom to return to Jerusalem but refuses to see him for two years — satisfying neither justice (proper accountability for murder) nor mercy (genuine forgiveness and restored relationship). The half-measure is worse than either extreme would have been: full exile would have kept Absalom distant and his rebellion impossible; full restoration with genuine reconciliation might have redirected his ambitions. The middle path — physical presence without relational repair — gives Absalom the platform while removing the relationship that might have tempered his pride.
14.examples:
Then: The two-year period in which Absalom lives in Jerusalem without seeing the king's face is the period in which his rebellion is being silently organized. The absence of genuine relationship creates the void that political ambition fills. Every day of the king's avoidance is a day of Absalom's growing resentment.

Now: The chapter speaks to every pastoral situation where forgiveness is declared but relationship is withheld — where the form of reconciliation is performed without the substance. This is the most damaging form of spiritual management: it deceives everyone (including sometimes the manager) into thinking the problem is resolved when it has merely been suppressed. Genuine restoration requires the hard conversation, the genuine accounting, and the costly work of rebuilt trust — not just a formal gesture that satisfies protocol.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Joab perceives that David's heart goes out to Absalom. He arranges for a wise woman from Tekoa to tell David a parable designed to secure Absalom's return. David sees through the ruse but grants Absalom's return - with the condition that Absalom not appear before the king. Absalom waits two years, burns Joab's field to get his attention, and finally is brought before David in a formal reconciliation.
verseByVerse.theology: The woman of Tekoa's speech is a masterpiece of applied argument: she uses a parable about her own sons (fictional) to get David to articulate a principle of mercy, then applies it to Absalom. David recognizes Joab's hand behind it - Is the hand of Joab with you in all this? - but grants the petition anyway. Ferguson notes that the partial reconciliation that follows - Absalom in Jerusalem but not in the king's presence - is the worst possible outcome: close enough to build a following, far enough to build resentment.
verseByVerse.examples: Begg observes that Absalom's beauty is described at length in vv.25-26: no blemish, glorious hair. He is the picture of what a king should look like - just as Saul was. The narrator places the physical description here as a warning: the beauty that attracts Israel to Absalom is the mirror of his father's fatal attraction to Bathsheba.

verseByVerse.quote: So Joab arose and went to Geshur and brought Absalom to Jerusalem. And the king said, Let him dwell apart in his own house; he is not to come into my presence. So Absalom lived apart in his own house and did not come into the king's presence.
verseByVerse.commentary: The partial reconciliation is a political and personal disaster that looks like mercy. Absalom is home but excluded; the resentment this breeds will fuel a rebellion. Two years pass in this suspended state. Then Absalom burns Joab's barley field - the only way he can get the general's attention - to force a full audience with the king. The scene of Absalom prostrating himself and the king kissing him is formal and cold: it is the reconciliation of protocol, not of the heart. David has done what Joab asked; he has not done what love required. The five years of partial and withheld relationship have created the conditions for everything that follows.

15.title: Absalom's Rebellion and David's Flight
15.text: <sup>14</sup>Then David said to all his servants who were with him at Jerusalem, 'Arise, and let us flee, or else there will be no escape for us from Absalom.' <sup>30</sup>But David went up the ascent of the Mount of Olives, weeping as he went, barefoot and with his head covered. And all the people who were with him covered their heads, and they went up, weeping as they went. (ESV)
15.overview:
Chapter 15 is one of the most Christ-haunted chapters in the Old Testament. David flees Jerusalem up the Mount of Olives, weeping, barefoot, with his head covered — the posture of grief and humility, the posture of a king stripped of everything — and the image cannot be read without feeling the tremor of a later night on the same mountain, when the greater Son of David sweated blood and was betrayed by a trusted companion. The parallels between David's passion and Jesus' passion are too many and too precise to be coincidental: the beloved companion who betrays (Ahithophel/Judas), the weeping ascent, the crossing of the Kidron (v. 23; John 18:1), the trusted friends who remain faithful, the prayer on the other side.

Absalom's rebellion is the fullest expression of Nathan's prophecy: I will raise up evil against you out of your own house (12:11). Absalom has spent four years systematically stealing the hearts of Israel (v. 6) — waiting at the city gate, hearing grievances, suggesting that the king does not care, making himself the alternative. He is brilliant, beautiful, and completely without conscience about what he is doing. When the coup is launched, its initial success is overwhelming: David flees; the city goes to Absalom; Ahithophel defects. Only a small group of the truly loyal remain.

sections.title: Absalom Steals the Hearts of Israel
sections.commentary:
The conspiracy is four years in the making (v. 7, though the Hebrew is debated). Absalom's method is the method of every populist who has ever stolen a kingdom: he positions himself as the accessible alternative to the distant incumbent, makes himself available to everyone the existing system has disappointed, and builds loyalty by making people feel heard. He rises early, stands at the gate, intercepts people coming to the king for justice, hears their case sympathetically, then says: your claims are good and right, but there is no man designated by the king to hear you — implying that David does not care, while Absalom does. When people bow to him, he takes their hands and kisses them. He is personally present where David is personally absent. He steals the hearts of the men of Israel one handshake at a time.

The conspiracy launches from Hebron — deliberately chosen: it was David's first capital, the place of his own anointing. Absalom goes there under the guise of fulfilling a vow (which David permits without question — another failure of attentiveness), and from there sends secret messengers throughout Israel announcing that Absalom has become king. Ahithophel, David's most trusted counselor, defects to Absalom. The treachery is comprehensive: the son, the counselor, and (apparently) the majority of Israel. R. C. Sproul observes that Absalom's rebellion is the external form of the same pattern as David's sin: it begins with the cultivation of desire (for the kingdom), proceeds through secret planning, and executes through the betrayal of a relationship of trust. David and Absalom are more alike than either would have wanted to admit.

sections.title: The Weeping Ascent
sections.commentary:
David's departure from Jerusalem is one of the most moving passages in the entire Bible. He leaves quickly — better to leave than to have the city destroyed — with a remarkable collection of the faithful: all his servants, the Cherethites and Pelethites (his elite guard), the Gittites who have followed him from Gath (foreign mercenaries whose loyalty is extraordinary), and Zadok and Abiathar the priests with the ark. The ark David decides to send back: carry the ark of God back into the city. If I find favor in the eyes of the LORD, he will bring me back and let me see both it and his dwelling place. But if he says, I have no delight in you, behold, here I am, let him do to me what seems good to him (vv. 25–26). This is the David of chapter 6 in the worst possible moment: he will not treat the ark as a talisman, will not carry it into battle for good luck. He releases it to God's decision, as he releases his own fate.

The ascent of the Mount of Olives — barefoot, head covered, weeping — is one of Scripture's most poignant images of humility. The greatest king of Israel, stripped of his kingdom by his own son, goes up the mountain weeping. Every Jew who later walked that road would have known the story; every Christian who reads it hears the echo of another night on the same mountain, when the Son of David went up the same slope in anguish, with a group of loyal but bewildered followers, to face the betrayal of one who had eaten at his table and walked with him for three years. The Gethsemane connection is not a pious overlay; it is structural: the king betrayed by his trusted counselor, ascending the mountain in grief, releasing the outcome to God's will. David's passion narrative is Jesus' passion narrative in shadow.

sections.title: Faithful Friends and Surprising Loyalty
sections.commentary:
Two figures stand out in the chapter's second half as models of covenant loyalty. Ittai the Gittite, when David tells him to go back — you are a foreigner, this is not your quarrel — responds with words that echo Ruth's: As the LORD lives, and as my lord the king lives, wherever my lord the king shall be, whether in death or life, even there also will your servant be (v. 21). A Gittite mercenary (from Gath — Goliath's hometown) speaks the language of covenant loyalty at the moment when Israel's own counselors are defecting. The foreigners remain when the insiders flee. This is the consistent pattern of the marginalized being more faithful than the privileged in Israel's story: Ruth, Uriah, Ittai.

Hushai the Arkite, David's friend, offers to go with him into exile; David sends him back to be a spy in Absalom's court, praying: O LORD, please turn the counsel of Ahithophel into foolishness (v. 31). The prayer is specific and strategic: David knows the only human counter to Ahithophel's counsel is another counselor of equal brilliance. He sends Hushai back — to Jerusalem, to Absalom, to the dangerous position of double agent — in the same spirit in which he sent the ark back: releasing the outcome to God's decision while using all available means. This is the consistent David at his best: praying specifically while acting strategically, trusting God's sovereignty while doing everything within human power to cooperate with it. Alistair Begg writes that David's prayer on the Mount of Olives ascent — one line, specific, immediately followed by action — is the model of urgent crisis prayer: not long, not elaborated, not trying to inform God of the situation he already knows, but simply asking for the specific thing needed and then acting in trust that the prayer has been heard.

15.theology: The King's Passion: A Shadow of Gethsemane. Chapter 15's ascent of the Mount of Olives is the single most Christologically charged passage in 2 Samuel. The structural parallels to Gethsemane are striking: the betrayal by a trusted companion, the night crossing of the Kidron valley (John 18:1 — Jesus crossed the Kidron; v. 23 — David crossed the Kidron), the weeping ascent of the Mount of Olives, the small group of loyal disciples, the prayer of release to the Father's will, the disciples who fall asleep (David's men weep but cannot ultimately prevent what is coming). The lesser David's passion narrative is the preparation for the greater David's passion narrative. John Calvin notes that the OT king's sufferings regularly prefigure the Christ's — not because they earn anything but because the shape of redemptive suffering is consistent: the righteous king is brought low before he is exalted.
15.examples:
Then: The faithfulness of Ittai the Gittite, Hushai the Arkite, the Levitical priests with the ark, the Cherethites and Pelethites — the king's loyal remnant in the hour of his greatest public humiliation — is the chapter's counterpoint to the mass defection of Israel. The question every person in David's entourage answered that day was: whose kingdom am I actually living for? The ones who stayed with David answered: his.

Now: The chapter challenges every professing Christian: when the kingdom of God appears to be losing, when following Christ is publicly costly rather than socially advantageous, will you stay with the King? The Ittai moment — 'as the LORD lives, wherever my lord the king shall be, whether in death or life, there also will your servant be' — is the language of discipleship, made most real not when it is easy but when the king is weeping and barefoot on the mountain.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Absalom systematically builds a following over four years: rising early, intercepting those coming to the king for judgment, sympathizing with their cases, lamenting that there is no one to listen, kissing those who bow to him. He steals the hearts of Israel. Then he requests permission to go to Hebron, under pretense of a vow, and launches his rebellion there.
verseByVerse.theology: Absalom's campaign is a political masterwork and a moral catastrophe. He identifies a real weakness in David's administration - access to justice - and exploits it by positioning himself as the remedy. MacArthur notes that the best deceptions work by mixing genuine grievance with self-serving ambition. The people's hearts are won not by Absalom's virtue but by their unmet needs and his attentiveness.
verseByVerse.examples: Keller observes that Absalom's four-year campaign of image-building reveals his true character: he is patient when it serves his purposes, charming when it advances his goals, and utterly ruthless when the moment comes. The man who could wait four years to steal a kingdom could also sacrifice everything that got in his way.

verseByVerse.quote: And Absalom used to rise early and stand beside the way of the gate. And when any man had a dispute to come before the king for judgment, Absalom would call to him and say, From what city are you? And when he said, Your servant is of such and such a tribe in Israel, Absalom would say to him, See, your claims are good and right, but there is no man designated by the king to hear you... So Absalom stole the hearts of the men of Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary: The theft of Israel's hearts is methodical: chariots, horses, running men - the trappings of kingship. Early rising - while David sleeps. Intercepting petitioners before they reach the gate. Validating everyone's complaint. Lamenting the absence of a judge - himself implicitly offered as the solution. The kissing of those who bow creates an intimacy that contrasts sharply with the formal distance of the court. Absalom is manufacturing a movement, and it works. After four years, the moment comes: he requests permission to go to Hebron to pay a vow, and 200 unsuspecting men go with him, and the conspiracy is unleashed.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: News reaches David: the hearts of Israel have gone after Absalom. David immediately orders his household to flee Jerusalem. He leaves with his servants, his household, the Cherethites and Pelethites, and 600 Gittites. The priests carry the ark out; David sends it back. He instructs Hushai to go back and counter Ahithophel's counsel.
verseByVerse.theology: David's response to the rebellion is remarkable for what it reveals about his character. He does not fight for the city; he flees weeping, barefoot, with his head covered - the posture of mourning. When Shimei curses him and his servants want to remove Shimei's head, David says: the LORD has told him to curse David; perhaps the LORD will see my affliction and repay me with good for his cursing today. This is a man who has accepted that his suffering is part of God's sovereign ordering.
verseByVerse.examples: Ferguson notes the instruction to return the ark to Jerusalem: If I find favor in the eyes of the LORD, he will bring me back and let me see both it and his dwelling place. But if he says, I have no delight in you, behold, here I am; let him do to me what seems good to him. This is submission to divine sovereignty in its purest form: not presuming on grace, but resting in God's good pleasure.

verseByVerse.quote: And all the country wept aloud as all the people passed by, and the king crossed the brook Kidron, and all the people passed on toward the wilderness. And David went up the ascent of the Mount of Olives, weeping as he went, barefoot and with his head covered. And all the people who were with him covered their heads, and they went up, weeping as they went.
verseByVerse.commentary: The procession up the Mount of Olives, weeping and barefoot, is one of the most poignant scenes in 2 Samuel. David, the king whose songs fill the Psalter, the man after God's own heart, is walking away from his throne barefoot with ashes on his head. The rabbis connected this to the prophecy of Zechariah 14, and the early church saw in it a type of Christ's own via dolorosa. David's submission to God's sovereign disposition of his kingdom is the measure of how far his repentance in chapter 12 has reached: he is not fighting God's judgment; he is accepting it.

16.title: Shimei's Curse and Absalom in Jerusalem
16.text: <sup>11</sup>David said to Abishai and to all his servants, 'Behold, my own son seeks my life; how much more now may this Benjaminite! Leave him alone, and let him curse, for the LORD has told him to. <sup>22</sup>So they pitched a tent for Absalom on the roof. And Absalom went in to his father's concubines in the sight of all Israel. (ESV)
16.overview:
Chapter 16 brings two encounters that test David's character in opposite ways: Ziba's slander (which David believes too quickly) and Shimei's cursing (which David receives with remarkable grace). The chapter also records Absalom's public violation of David's concubines on the palace roof — the fulfillment of Nathan's specific prophecy (I will take your wives before your eyes and give them to your neighbor, 12:11–12) — and ends with Ahithophel's counsel accepted and its devastating implications set in motion.

The theological center of the chapter is David's response to Shimei. The Benjaminite throws stones and curses and calls David a man of blood; Abishai offers to go and take his head; and David says: leave him alone. If he is cursing because the LORD has said to him, Curse David, who then shall say, Why have you done so? (v. 10). This is not passivity but theology: David, stripped of everything, receiving a curse he partly deserves, accepting it as coming through God's permission, and refusing to answer curse with violence. It is one of the most gracious responses to unjust criticism in the entire Bible — and one of the most Christ-like moments in David's story.

sections.title: Ziba's Slander and David's Hasty Judgment
sections.commentary: Ziba arrives with provisions and a story: Mephibosheth, he says, has stayed in Jerusalem expecting to be restored to his grandfather Saul's kingdom now that David's house is in chaos. The story is plausible on its face and entirely false — as chapter 19:24–30 will reveal, Mephibosheth neither groomed himself nor changed his sandals from the day David departed until his safe return, in mourning. But David, fleeing in crisis, exhausted and likely suspicious of everyone, believes Ziba immediately and gives him all Mephibosheth's land. The hasty judgment is understandable under pressure; it is still a failure of the justice that chapter 8:15 praised David for administering to all his people. Crisis reveals the limits of even the best character — the king who could administer equity with patience in stable times makes a snap decision under pressure that wrongs the covenant recipient of his greatest act of grace.

sections.title: Shimei's Curse and David's Grace
sections.commentary:
Shimei's cursing is sustained, public, and escalating: he throws stones, throws dirt, and calls David a man of blood, a worthless man, attributing all his troubles to God's judgment on his treatment of the house of Saul. Much of this is false or distorted; David was not bloodguilty toward Saul. But Abishai's offer to remove his head is refused with a response that ranks among the most spiritually mature in the entire David narrative: If he is cursing because the LORD has said to him, Curse David, who then shall say, Why have you done so? Behold, my own son seeks my life; how much more now may this Benjaminite! Leave him alone, and let him curse, for the LORD has told him to. It may be that the LORD will look on my affliction and that the LORD will repay me with good for his cursing today.

This is David at the bottom of his circumstances and the top of his theology. He has lost his kingdom, his city, his household, his counselor. He is being stoned and cursed by a man he could easily have removed. And he is reading the situation through the lens of God's sovereignty: perhaps the LORD has directed even this. Perhaps God can be trusted to repay the humiliation with good in his own time. The same David who danced before the LORD in triumph now walks through shame with the same confidence in divine sovereignty. R. C. Sproul writes that this moment is the clearest evidence in the entire OT of what genuine surrender to God's providence looks like at the experiential level: accepting even unjust suffering as coming within God's permission, not because it is just but because God is sovereign and can be trusted to work even this for good.

The Christological resonance is unmistakable: Jesus, on his way to the cross, does not call down twelve legions of angels (Matt. 26:53); he accepts the cup the Father gives, including the unjust cursing, the false accusations, the spitting and mockery, with the same theology David expresses here: it may be that the Father will look on this affliction and repay good for evil. Peter's first epistle — when he was reviled, he did not revile in return; when he suffered, he did not threaten, but continued entrusting himself to him who judges justly (1 Pet. 2:23) — is the NT commentary on David's response to Shimei.

sections.title: Ahithophel's Counsel and the Fulfillment of Prophecy
sections.commentary: Absalom's entry into Jerusalem with Ahithophel is the high tide of the rebellion. Hushai's apparently convincing performance of defection (Long live the king! Long live the king!) gains him Absalom's confidence for the moment. Ahithophel's first piece of counsel — lie with your father's concubines on the palace roof, publicly — is accepted. And Nathan's word from chapter 12:11–12 is fulfilled with surgical precision: I will take your wives before your eyes and give them to your neighbor, and he shall lie with your wives in the sight of this sun. For you did it secretly, but I will do this thing before all Israel and before the sun. David did it in secret; the consequence is played out in public. The concubines who will spend the rest of their lives in widowed seclusion (20:3) are the innocent victims of David's original sin, carried all the way to its predicted consequence. The word of God, once spoken through Nathan, cannot be deflected. Alistair Begg notes that the fulfillment is not satisfying but sobering: the God who forgives sin does not always prevent its natural and predicted consequences from running their full course.

16.theology: Receiving Unjust Suffering as God's Appointment. David's response to Shimei is the chapter's theological gift. He does not justify the curse — Shimei is largely wrong about the facts — but he accepts even unjust treatment as coming within the permission of God's sovereign care, and he trusts that the same God who allows the cursing can repay it with good. This is the theology of the cross applied to ordinary suffering: not every unpleasant experience is deserved, but every unpleasant experience can be entrusted to the God who is sovereign over all of them.
16.examples:
Then: The chapter shows David maintaining theological clarity in three different kinds of pressure: Ziba's manipulation (he fails here), Shimei's cursing (he succeeds here), and Absalom's usurpation (he accepts the consequences with grace). The mixed record is honest: even the best character has its weak points, and crisis exposes which principles are deeply held and which are held only when comfortable.

Now: The Shimei episode is perhaps the most practically useful model in the chapter: the response to unjust criticism and public shaming that neither retaliates nor suppresses, that receives even false accusations as coming under God's providential permission, and that trusts God to vindicate in his own time. Paul's instruction — bless those who curse you, do not repay evil for evil (Rom. 12:14, 17) — is David's Shimei-theology in apostolic form.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1-14 - Ziba, Shimei, and David's Submission
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Ziba meets David with provisions and lies about Mephibosheth. David gives Mephibosheth's estate to Ziba. Shimei of the house of Saul curses David and throws stones. David's nephew Abishai wants to cut off Shimei's head; David restrains him.
verseByVerse.theology: David's response to Shimei's curses is theologically profound: let him alone, and let him curse, for the LORD has told him to. He does not know whether God has told Shimei anything of the sort, but he receives the curses as potentially God's voice through a human instrument. This is not passivity or despair; it is a willingness to let God speak through unexpected channels, even hostile ones. MacArthur notes that this posture - open to rebuke even from enemies - is one of the marks of genuine humility.
verseByVerse.examples: Begg observes that the Ziba episode introduces an ambiguity that will not be resolved until chapter 19: has Mephibosheth betrayed David, or has Ziba lied to get the estate? David acts on Ziba's information; he may have been deceived. The unresolved tension is realistic: in crisis, we often act on incomplete information and must live with the consequences.

verseByVerse.quote: And the king said, What do you mean? Shimei said, The LORD has avenged on you all the blood of the house of Saul, in whose place you have reigned... But Abishai the son of Zeruiah said to the king, Why should this dead dog curse my lord the king? Let me go over and take off his head. The king said, What have I to do with you, you sons of Zeruiah? If he is cursing because the LORD has said to him, Curse David, who then shall say, Why have you done so?
verseByVerse.commentary: The contrast between Abishai and David is a recurring theme in 2 Samuel: the sons of Zeruiah are always ready for immediate violent retribution; David consistently restrains them and looks for God's hand in apparent injustice. Shimei's curses are personal and theologically garbled - David did not murder Saul's house - but David receives them with a question: perhaps the LORD will repay me with good for his cursing today. He is not certain; he is humble. The king who has walked away from his throne barefoot continues to walk in the dust while stones and curses rain down on him.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Absalom enters Jerusalem with Ahithophel. Hushai presents himself to Absalom and is accepted. Ahithophel advises Absalom to sleep with David's concubines on the palace roof - publicly, fulfilling Nathan's prophecy. The counsel is taken.
verseByVerse.theology: Ahithophel's advice is the precise fulfillment of Nathan's word: I will take your wives before your eyes and give them to your neighbor, and he shall lie with your wives in the sight of this sun (12:11). The prophecy is enacted by Absalom's own pride and Ahithophel's counsel. MacArthur notes that the public nature of the act is required by its purpose: it signals to all Israel that the breach between Absalom and David is irreparable. There is no reconciliation possible after this.
verseByVerse.examples: Ferguson observes that Ahithophel's counsel is described at the end of verse 23 as if it were an oracle from God - his word was so trusted. This heightens the drama of the next chapter: when Hushai's inferior military counsel is accepted over Ahithophel's superior counsel, it is because the LORD had ordained to defeat the good counsel of Ahithophel.

verseByVerse.quote: And Ahithophel said to Absalom, Go in to your father's concubines, whom he has left to keep the house, and all Israel will hear that you have made yourself a stench to your father, and the hands of all who are with you will be strengthened. So they pitched a tent for Absalom on the roof. And Absalom went in to his father's concubines in the sight of all Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary: The tent on the roof where David had seen Bathsheba is now the place where Absalom publicly claims his father's concubines. The irony is precise and terrible: the same rooftop, the same public visibility, a different generation of sin. Nathan's word has come to pass. The concubines are victims twice over - of David's sin in the original chapter and of Absalom's political theater now. They will live out their lives in isolation after David returns (20:3): guarded like widows, alive without life. The cost of David's sin extends far beyond David himself.

17.title: Ahithophel's Counsel Overthrown
17.text: <sup>14</sup>And Absalom and all the men of Israel said, 'The counsel of Hushai the Arkite is better than the counsel of Ahithophel.' For the LORD had ordained to defeat the good counsel of Ahithophel, so that the LORD might bring harm upon Absalom. (ESV)
17.overview:
Chapter 17 is the chapter where David's prayer — O LORD, please turn the counsel of Ahithophel into foolishness (15:31) — is answered in precise and remarkable detail. Ahithophel's counsel (strike David quickly, tonight, before he can regroup) is brilliant military strategy that would probably have worked. Hushai's counter-counsel (gather all Israel and strike in overwhelming force when the time is right) is strategically inferior but politically seductive — it appeals to Absalom's vanity and his desire for a decisive, triumphant battle. Absalom chooses Hushai's counsel. And the narrator supplies the theological interpretation: the LORD had ordained to defeat the good counsel of Ahithophel, so that the LORD might bring harm upon Absalom.

The answer to David's prayer comes through the persuasiveness of a spy's argument, through the vanity of a proud rebel, and through the desperate courage of two young women who carry the message past Absalom's searchers in a well. Providence working through ordinary human means — a spy's eloquence, a woman's quick thinking, a well in a man's courtyard — is the consistent divine signature of this chapter and of the entire Absalom narrative. Ahithophel, recognizing that his counsel has been rejected and that the rebellion will fail, goes home, sets his house in order, and hangs himself. His death anticipates Judas's death with chilling precision.

sections.title: Two Counsels Before the Rebel King
sections.commentary:
Ahithophel's counsel is described with superlatives: it was as if he consulted the word of God (16:23). His plan — twelve thousand men, tonight, strike David while he is weary and frightened, kill only the king, return all the people to Absalom — is exactly right militarily. It would have worked. Absalom had the force, the speed, the element of surprise. David, exhausted and demoralized, was vulnerable in the precise way Ahithophel described.

Hushai's counter-argument is a masterwork of calculated misdirection. He appeals to Absalom's pride — your father is a mighty warrior, his men are fierce fighters, the initial strike will cause a panic that will turn Israel against you. Then he appeals to Absalom's vanity — wait, gather all Israel from Dan to Beersheba like the sand of the sea, and go into battle yourself, so that the glory is yours. The argument is designed to produce delay, and it works. The council chooses Hushai's counsel — and the narrator immediately supplies the interpretive key: the LORD had ordained this. The human mechanism is Hushai's eloquence and Absalom's pride; the efficient cause is God's sovereign answer to David's specific prayer.

Ahithophel's immediate recognition that the rebellion has failed, and his orderly response — he goes home, sets his affairs in order, and hangs himself — is one of the most chilling moments in the book. He is not a fool; he knows exactly what the rejection of his counsel means for the outcome. Like Judas, he cannot live with the knowledge of what he has done and what it will cost. And like Judas, his death is orderly, premeditated, and utterly lonely. The man who was called almost-divine in his wisdom ends his life in the darkness of his own room, with no one to whom he can turn.

sections.title: The Warning Carried to David
sections.commentary:
Hushai immediately recognizes the danger of the delay: even with Absalom's vanity buying time, David must be warned to cross the Jordan immediately. The message is carried by two young women — Ahimaaz and Jonathan, the sons of the priests, who have been waiting at En-rogel for intelligence — through a network of courier that includes a woman who conceals them in a well under grain, then misleads Absalom's searchers with a casual lie. The courage of the ordinary people in this network — the woman at the well, the priests' sons risking detection — is the human face of God's providential care for his anointed.

David crosses the Jordan that night with all his people. On the other side, he receives provisions from Shobi (an Ammonite), Machir (who had sheltered Mephibosheth), and Barzillai the Gileadite — three men from outside David's core constituency who supply food, bedding, and equipment for the army. The list is itself a statement: the king who is fleeing from his own son is being sustained by those who are outside the inner circle of Israel, and sustained generously. The marginalized continue to be more faithful than the privileged. Tim Keller observes that the chapter is a sustained demonstration of Romans 8:28 in narrative form: every human decision, every act of courage, every providential delay, and every logistical provision is being worked together for good by the God who answered a prayer on the Mount of Olives.

17.theology: Providence Through Ordinary Means. Chapter 17 is the fullest illustration in 2 Samuel of how God answers specific prayer through ordinary human means. The prayer was: turn Ahithophel's counsel into foolishness. The answer was: a spy's eloquent argument + a rebel's vanity + a woman's quick thinking + a courier network + the crossing of the Jordan. No angel appeared; no miracle was performed. God worked through the grain of human personality and circumstance to accomplish exactly what he had been asked to accomplish. This is the consistent testimony of Scripture about providence: it operates ordinarily more than extraordinarily, through the weave of human choice and circumstance rather than above it.
17.examples:
Then: Ahithophel's suicide is the chapter's darkest note — the brilliant counselor who was almost-divine in his wisdom ends by its failure. The man whose counsel was sought by kings could not counsel himself through the collapse of his ambitions. Wisdom that is not anchored in the fear of God collapses when its projects fail, because those projects were its only ground of meaning.

Now: The chapter encourages the believer whose specific prayer seems to require extraordinary means to trust that God's ordinary means are sufficient. The well in the courtyard, the woman with the grain, the crossed-the-Jordan night — these are enough. God does not need spectacular interventions to accomplish his purposes; he needs only one praying king on a mountain and the ordinary cooperating movements of human choice and circumstance.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Ahithophel counsels immediate pursuit of David with a strike force tonight. Hushai, David's spy, urges delay - appeal to Absalom's vanity about leading a massive army himself. Absalom chooses Hushai's counsel. Ahithophel, seeing his counsel rejected, goes home and hangs himself. Hushai gets word to David to cross the Jordan immediately.
verseByVerse.theology: The decisive verse is verse 14: the LORD had ordained to defeat the good counsel of Ahithophel, so that the LORD might bring harm upon Absalom. Ahithophel's counsel was militarily superior; Hushai's was inferior. But God works through the pride of Absalom and the eloquence of Hushai to accomplish his purpose. Ferguson notes that this is one of the clearest statements in the historical books of divine sovereignty working through secondary causes - human pride, persuasive speech, the vanity of kings.
verseByVerse.examples: Kidner observes that Ahithophel's suicide is the act of a man who understands military strategy well enough to know that his counsel, if rejected, meant the rebellion would fail. He goes home, puts his house in order, and hangs himself. He appears again in Psalm 41 and 55 as the trusted companion whose betrayal wounded David like a sword. His end is a type of Judas, both in his counsel against God's anointed and in his self-destruction when the counsel was overturned.

verseByVerse.quote: And Absalom and all the men of Israel said, The counsel of Hushai the Archite is better than the counsel of Ahithophel. For the LORD had ordained to defeat the good counsel of Ahithophel, so that the LORD might bring harm upon Absalom.
verseByVerse.commentary: Ahithophel's counsel was correct: strike now, tonight, while David is exhausted and his men discouraged. A small, fast-moving force against a tired king with 600 men. Hushai appeals to Absalom's imagination and ego: you know your father and his men, they are mighty men; you should lead all Israel yourself, as the sand by the sea. Absalom chooses the vision that flatters him. The narrator does not leave the outcome to chance; he states it plainly: the LORD had ordained it. Providence works through human choice and human vanity to protect the man God has chosen. David crosses the Jordan that night.

18.title: The Death of Absalom
18.text: <sup>14</sup>Joab said, 'I will not waste time like this with you.' And he took three javelins in his hand and thrust them into the heart of Absalom while he was still alive in the oak. <sup>33</sup>And the king was deeply moved and went up to the chamber over the gate and wept. And as he went, he said, 'O my son Absalom, my son, my son Absalom! Would I had died instead of you, O Absalom, my son, my son!' (ESV)
18.overview:
Chapter 18 contains two of the most powerful scenes in the entire Bible: Absalom caught in the oak tree, and David's lament. Both are devastating, each in a different way. Absalom — the beautiful rebel, the long-haired usurper — is caught by his famous hair in the branches of an oak while fleeing the battle, left hanging there helplessly, and killed by Joab despite David's explicit command to deal gently with him. And David, waiting at the city gate for news of the battle, receives the news that the battle is won — and hears, in the same breath, that Absalom is dead. And his response: O my son Absalom, my son, my son Absalom! Would I had died instead of you, O Absalom, my son, my son!

The lament is simultaneously one of the most human and one of the most Christologically significant passages in the book. It is human: the grief of a father for a son who died in rebellion, the wish to have died instead, the love that cannot be extinguished by betrayal. It is Christological: the greater Son of David, who died in place of rebels who did not want him, whose death was the substitutionary death that all of David's lament only wished for and could not provide. David wished he could have died instead of Absalom; the Son of David actually died instead of those who rebelled against him, and his death accomplished what David's death could not have — genuine redemption rather than merely imagined substitution.

sections.title: David's Command and Joab's Disobedience
sections.commentary:
David's command — deal gently for my sake with the young man Absalom — is both a father's plea and a king's order, and it is disobeyed by Joab with characteristic calculation. When told that Absalom is hanging in the oak, Joab asks why the soldier didn't kill him; the soldier invokes the king's command; Joab dismisses it and kills Absalom himself with three javelins. His reasoning is unstated but clear: Absalom alive is a perpetual political threat to David's kingdom, and whatever the king's personal grief, the kingdom is safer with Absalom dead.

Joab is not entirely wrong about the political calculation — Absalom would have remained a rallying point for future rebellion. But he is entirely wrong about his authority: the king's command was clear. Joab has now disobeyed David twice to commit murder (Abner, Absalom) and will do so once more (Amasa, 20:10). He is the most consistent moral problem of David's kingdom — the man whose military pragmatism and political calculation repeatedly override the covenantal principles of the king he serves. David is incapable of punishing him while he needs him, and the grief this constraint produces is one of the lasting wounds of his reign.

Absalom's death — caught by his hair in an oak, killed while hanging helpless — has a quality of the grotesque that the narrator does not soften. The beautiful rebel who cultivated his hair as a symbol of royal identity (he weighed it annually, 14:26) is caught by that very hair and killed hanging above the ground. There is a poetic justice in the detail: the thing he was proudest of became the instrument of his capture. The pillar he had erected in the King's Valley — a monument to his own name because he had no son to carry it — stands beside the narrator's account of his death as an irony: the man who built his own monument died leaving no legacy except the destruction he caused.

sections.title: The Messengers and the Gate
sections.commentary:
The scene at the city gate — David waiting, two runners approaching, the watchman calling their approach, David's single question about Absalom — is narrated with extraordinary suspense and delicacy. Ahimaaz runs first and arrives first, but deflects the question about Absalom: I saw a great commotion... but I do not know what it was. The Cushite runner arrives second and tells the truth: may the enemies of my lord the king and all who rise up against you for evil be like that young man. The euphemism cannot soften the verdict. Absalom is dead.

David's question throughout the waiting — Is it well with the young man Absalom? — reveals everything about his state. The battle's outcome is secondary to him; his concern is entirely for his son. Joab's fury in chapter 19 — the king has turned the day's victory into mourning — is understandable from a military perspective. But David is not, in this moment, operating from political calculation; he is operating from paternal grief. The father who loved his son imperfectly, managed his son's rebellion incompetently, and contributed by his own failures to the conditions that made the rebellion possible, receives the news of his son's death with a grief that overwhelms the victory.

sections.title: The Lament: A Father for a Son
sections.commentary:
The lament — eight Hebrew words, repeated twice: O my son Absalom, my son, my son Absalom! Would I had died instead of you, O Absalom, my son, my son! — is one of the most compressed and most piercing expressions of grief in Scripture. Every word carries weight. My son, five times: this is not a rebel, not a threat, not a political problem — this is his son. Would I had died instead of you: the wish for substitution, the desire of love to absorb the death of the beloved. The repetition is not rhetoric; it is the way grief actually speaks — circling back to the same words, unable to move beyond them, unable to find a new language for the magnitude of the loss.

Tim Keller writes that David's lament is the most direct OT anticipation of the heart of the gospel. David wishes he could have died instead of Absalom; the Son of David actually died instead of those who were in rebellion against him, who had stolen the hearts of Israel away from the true King, who had tried to seize the throne that was not theirs. The difference is that David's substitution was impossible — he could not die instead of Absalom and accomplish anything — while Christ's substitution was both possible and efficacious. His death in place of rebels actually accomplished their reconciliation. David's 'would I had died instead of you' is the longing of a father's love reaching toward what only the cross could provide. Every Good Friday sermon should spend time at David's gate.

18.theology: The Father's Heart and the Son's Death. David's lament over Absalom is the most direct human analogy in Scripture to the Father's grief over the lost and the Son's death for those who rebelled. The love David bears for Absalom — the son who tried to kill him, who violated his concubines, who stole his kingdom — is the love that refuses to be ended by betrayal, that would rather absorb the death than watch the beloved perish. It cannot save Absalom; only the Son of David's actual death can save the rebels who come to him in genuine repentance. But the shape of the love — the wish to die instead of the beloved — maps exactly onto the cross: God shows his love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us (Rom. 5:8).
18.examples:
Then: Joab's disobedience of David's explicit command to deal gently with Absalom is the chapter's moral problem alongside its emotional center. The king whose grief at chapter's end is overwhelming is the same king who could not prevent a subordinate from overriding his most personal order. The constraints of political necessity over genuine authority is one of the most painful realities of leadership, and David experiences it at its most costly.

Now: The chapter speaks to every parent whose child has died in rebellion — not merely physical rebellion but spiritual, relational, or moral. The love David bears for Absalom, which neither the rebellion nor the death could extinguish, is the image of a love that is not conditional on the beloved's behavior. The gospel does not say God loved us when we were lovable; it says he loved us while we were rebels. David's grief models that unconditional love in its most human and most costly form.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: David musters his forces. The people insist he stay behind. He commands his generals: Deal gently for my sake with the young man Absalom. The battle goes badly for Absalom's forces. Absalom is caught by his head in an oak tree and left hanging. Joab, against David's explicit command, drives three spears through Absalom's heart.
verseByVerse.theology: David's command - Deal gently for my sake with the young man Absalom - is the expression of a father's love that overrides all political and military logic. Joab ignores it. Joab's act is militarily rational: a living Absalom is an eternal threat to David's throne. Joab is also right that delay is dangerous: he rebukes the soldier who would not strike, noting that Joab would have given him ten pieces of silver. But MacArthur notes that Joab consistently acts as if the ends justify the means - a pattern that will eventually cost him his life.
verseByVerse.examples: Ferguson observes that Absalom's death by hanging in an oak tree - his magnificent hair, his glory, caught in the branches of a tree - is a kind of ironic justice. The man whose glory was his hair is destroyed by his glory. The man who wanted to be king is buried in a pit in the forest under a heap of stones, unlike the monument he had built for himself in the king's valley.

verseByVerse.quote: And the king ordered Joab and Abishai and Ittai, Spare the young man Absalom for my sake. And all the people heard when the king gave orders to all the commanders about Absalom. And the battle was in the forest of Ephraim.
verseByVerse.commentary: The battle in the forest of Ephraim turns against Absalom: the forest devoured more people that day than the sword. Absalom himself is riding his mule and the mule passes under a great oak and his head catches in the oak, and he is left hanging between heaven and earth while his mule rides on. The image is memorable and terrible: the beautiful prince suspended between earth and sky, caught by his own glory, helpless. When told, Joab asks why the soldier did not kill him. The soldier quotes the king's own command. Joab takes three spears and drives them into Absalom's heart while he still lives. Then ten armor-bearers surround him and strike him dead.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Ahimaaz wants to run with the news of victory but Joab sends the Cushite first. Ahimaaz runs and arrives first but withholds the news about Absalom. The Cushite arrives and David asks the same question: Is the young man Absalom safe? He hears the answer, goes to his chamber, and weeps: O my son Absalom, my son, my son Absalom! Would I had died instead of you, O Absalom, my son, my son!
verseByVerse.theology: David's grief is one of the most raw expressions of parental love in all of literature. The military victory becomes a personal catastrophe. Would I had died instead of you is the language of substitution - a father who would bear his son's death in his place. Keller notes that this lament echoes across Scripture: it is the language of covenant love that takes the death of the beloved upon itself. The Father who sends his Son does not lament - but the Son who cries My God, my God, why have you forsaken me? bears the weight of what no human father could.
verseByVerse.examples: Sproul notes the irony of Joab's rebuke to David in the next chapter: the victory parade requires David to appear, or the people who saved his life will feel shamed. The king who should be celebrating is weeping. And both are right: the victory is real, and the grief is real, and holding both together is one of the most human moments in the Bible.

verseByVerse.quote: And the king was deeply moved and went up to the chamber over the gate and wept. And as he went, he said, O my son Absalom, my son, my son Absalom! Would I had died instead of you, O Absalom, my son, my son!
verseByVerse.commentary: The runner's race, the anxious king at the gate, the question he can't stop asking: Is it well with the young man Absalom? The Cushite's diplomatic answer - May the enemies of my lord the king and all who rise up against you for evil be like that young man - is understood immediately. David goes up to the chamber over the gate and weeps. The king is not weeping for his kingdom, his throne, his generals. He is weeping for the son who rebelled against him, shamed him, tried to kill him, lay with his concubines in public - and who is gone. The love is excessive by every political and moral calculation. It is the love of a father for a son, uncalculating and inconsolable.

19.title: The Return of the King
19.text: <sup>4</sup>The king covered his face, and the king cried with a loud voice, 'O my son Absalom, O Absalom, my son, my son!' <sup>14</sup>And he swayed the heart of all the men of Judah as one man, so that they sent word to the king, 'Return, you and all your servants.' (ESV)
19.overview:
Chapter 19 is the return — but a return complicated by grief, by grievances, by the unresolved tensions that the rebellion has left in its wake. David's public mourning for Absalom has turned the victory into mourning for the whole army, and Joab intervenes with characteristic bluntness: get up, face your people, or you will have no people left to return to. David obeys. The journey home involves encounters that each represent a different kind of unresolved relationship: Shimei seeking pardon, Mephibosheth's grievance against Ziba's slander, Barzillai the old Gileadite declining the king's invitation, and the dispute between Judah and Israel over who has the greater right to escort the king home.

The chapter is a study in the messy, incomplete nature of post-crisis restoration. The king returns; the relationships are partially repaired; justice is partly done and partly deferred. David pardons Shimei (against his better instincts, and against Solomon's eventual judgment in 1 Kings 2). He half-resolves the Mephibosheth-Ziba dispute by splitting the land. He honors Barzillai's gracious refusal with warm farewell. The restoration is real but partial — and the final dispute between Judah and Israel over the king's escort plants the seed of the next rebellion (Sheba's revolt in chapter 20).

sections.title: Joab's Rebuke and the King's Recovery
sections.commentary:
Joab's confrontation of the grieving king is the most direct speech to David in the entire book, and it comes from the most morally compromised man in David's entourage. The man who disobeyed the king's command and killed Absalom is now rebuking the king for grieving Absalom's death. The irony is brutal: Joab created the grief he is now telling David to suppress. But his argument is not wrong: David's public mourning has communicated to the army that he values the rebel son more than the loyal soldiers who risked their lives for him. The soldiers who saved his kingdom are sneaking into the city as if they had done something shameful. The army's morale, and David's ability to lead, depend on his recovery.

David obeys Joab — a remarkable act of submission from a king to a disobedient general. He gets up, sits at the gate, and the word goes out. The army comes before the king. The recovery is willed, not spontaneous; David makes himself do what grief makes impossible to feel. This is the discipline of leadership: the obligation to function for others even when the personal cost is enormous. It is also, in a smaller way, the discipline of grief that Paul describes — grieve, but not as those without hope (1 Thess. 4:13). Grief is real; the duties of the living are also real; both truths must be honored. David's sitting at the gate is not the suppression of grief but its subordination to the claims of covenant responsibility.

sections.title: Shimei, Mephibosheth, and Barzillai
sections.commentary:
The three encounters on the road home represent three different kinds of relationship requiring resolution. Shimei comes with a thousand Benjaminites, throwing himself on the ground, confessing his sin of cursing the king. Abishai again wants to kill him; David again overrules him, and adds a significant reasoning: this is the day of my restoration, why should anyone be put to death in Israel today? The pardon is genuine in the moment — and David's instinct that it should hold (v. 23) is overridden by his eventual deathbed instruction to Solomon (1 Kings 2:8–9: remember what he did to me). The tension between genuine mercy and covenant justice is unresolved in David's lifetime.

Mephibosheth's appearance is one of the chapter's most affecting moments: he has not dressed his feet, trimmed his beard, or washed his clothes from the day David departed to the day of his return — the full expression of mourning for the king's absence. His explanation refutes Ziba's slander completely: Ziba deceived him, left him behind (his lameness made independent travel impossible), and lied about his loyalties. David's half-justice — giving half the land to each — is not Solomon's wisdom but it is not nothing; the acknowledgment that Ziba lied is partial vindication for the man who had done nothing wrong. Alistair Begg observes that this resolution leaves both men somewhat aggrieved — the grace of chapter 9 imperfectly restored — but Mephibosheth's response is the model of the person whose security does not depend on the outcome: let him take it all, since my lord the king has come home in peace. His joy at the king's return transcends the question of the land.

Barzillai's gracious refusal of David's invitation — I am eighty years old; what pleasure can I still taste? Let me die in my own city near the grave of my father and my mother — is one of the chapter's finest moments of self-knowledge. He is too old to enjoy the honor; he asks only to be permitted to escort the king a little way and then to return. His son Chimham goes in his place. The exchange is full of warmth and dignity: an old man who served the king in his hour of need and now graciously declines the reward, asking only to see the king home safely. David's farewell — all that you desire from me I will do for you — is the gratitude of a king for a servant who gave without calculating the return.

sections.title: The Quarrel Between Judah and Israel
sections.commentary:
The chapter ends with a quarrel that anticipates the final division of the kingdom: the men of Israel accuse Judah of stealing the king's return for themselves; Judah responds that the king is their relative; the argument escalates. The dispute is ostensibly about protocol — who has the right to escort the king — but it is really about tribal jealousy that runs deeper than the Absalom crisis and will eventually fracture the kingdom under Rehoboam. The quarrel is not resolved; it is simply interrupted by Sheba's rebellion in the next chapter.

The chapter's last exchange — the words of the men of Judah were fiercer than the words of the men of Israel — is a compressed warning. The kingdom has been restored; the seeds of its next fragmentation are already germinating. This is the consistent testimony of political life in a fallen world: every resolution carries within it the unresolved tensions that will produce the next crisis. The only kingdom that does not contain the seeds of its own disintegration is the eternal kingdom of the Son of David, in whom there is neither Jew nor Greek, neither Israel nor Judah, but all are one in Christ Jesus (Gal. 3:28).

19.theology: The King's Return as Restoration. David's return to Jerusalem has Christological resonances that the NT writers will develop fully: the king who was driven out by rebellion, who suffered in humiliation, who returned in triumph to restore the kingdom and receive the loyalty of those who had remained faithful. The encounters on the road — Shimei's pardon, Mephibosheth's vindication, Barzillai's farewell — are the king's first acts of grace upon return, the precedents he sets for the kind of kingdom he will restore. Each encounter is an act of mercy that prioritizes the day of salvation over the claims of strict justice.
19.examples:
Then: The chapter covers a full range of human responses to the returning king: the guilty seeking pardon (Shimei), the wronged seeking vindication (Mephibosheth), the loyal asking nothing but to see the king home safely (Barzillai), and the quarrelsome asserting their prior claim (Judah vs. Israel). All of these characters appear in the church's relationship with the returning King, and all of them are addressed by the grace that makes mercy available without pretending the past was different from what it was.

Now: The chapter's central message for the believer is the model of Mephibosheth: whatever the outcome of the land dispute, the king has come home in peace, and that is enough. The person whose joy at the King's presence exceeds their concern for their own vindication has understood the gospel. The kingdom is restored; sit at the table; the land will sort itself out.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Joab rebukes David for grieving instead of celebrating. David appears to the people. He negotiates his return with Judah and then with Israel. He deals with Shimei, with Mephibosheth's ambiguous case, with Barzillai's generosity. Dispute breaks out between Judah and Israel over who has the greater claim on the king.
verseByVerse.theology: The chapter is a political negotiation and a moral reckoning. David pardons Shimei despite Abishai's objections: Shall anyone be put to death in Israel this day? For do I not know that I am this day king over Israel? MacArthur observes that the magnanimity David shows to Shimei and Mephibosheth is the return of the same David who spared Saul twice. His power restored, he uses it with mercy rather than vengeance.
verseByVerse.examples: Begg observes that Mephibosheth's defense - he had not anointed his feet or trimmed his beard since the day the king departed until the day he came back in safety - suggests Ziba did indeed lie in chapter 16. David's compromise (split the land with Ziba) is not entirely satisfying, but it is the judgment of a man who cannot fully verify the claims and wants to be merciful to both.

verseByVerse.quote: And Joab came into the house to the king and said, You have today covered with shame the faces of all your servants, who have this day saved your life and the lives of your sons and daughters and wives and concubines, by loving those who hate you and hating those who love you... for I know that if Absalom were alive and all of us were dead today, then you would be pleased.
verseByVerse.commentary: Joab's rebuke is brutal and accurate: a king who mourns his defeated enemy publicly is telling his loyal servants that their sacrifice was unwelcome. The political damage is real. David appears at the gate; the people come before him. The return negotiation is messy and human: Judah and Israel argue about who owns the king. Shimei comes with a thousand Benjaminites, prostrating himself, begging mercy. David grants it, over Abishai's protest. Mephibosheth comes, unkempt from two weeks of mourning. His devotion seems real; Ziba's word seems false; David splits the land and moves on. Barzillai, who provided food at Mahanaim, declines to come to court in his old age and sends his son instead. The king kisses and blesses him. The narrative of return is as complicated as human life.

20.title: Sheba's Revolt and the Wise Woman of Abel
20.text: <sup>22</sup>Then the woman went to all the people in her wisdom. And they cut off the head of Sheba the son of Bichri and threw it out to Joab. So he blew the trumpet, and they dispersed from the city, every man to his home. And Joab returned to Jerusalem to the king. (ESV)
20.overview:
Chapter 20 brings the second rebellion of David's later years — shorter than Absalom's, resolved with a single act of wisdom, but revealing the extent to which the kingdom remains unstable. Sheba the Benjaminite, seizing on the tribal quarrel from chapter 19's ending, blows a trumpet and declares: We have no portion in David, and we have no inheritance in the son of Jesse; every man to his tents, O Israel! Most of Israel follows Sheba; Judah alone remains loyal. David sends Amasa (whom he has just appointed commander over the army, replacing Joab) to muster Judah. Amasa is slow; Joab takes the field, kills Amasa at Gibeon, pursues Sheba to Abel Beth-maacah. There, a wise woman negotiates from the city wall and delivers Sheba's head over the wall.

The chapter also resolves several outstanding administrative matters — the list of David's officials (vv. 23–26) mirrors the list in chapter 8, bookending the period of crisis and signaling that the kingdom has returned to normal operation. But Joab's murder of Amasa, added to his murder of Abner and Absalom, marks him as a man whose career has run well beyond what covenantal justice should permit. David deferred action; Solomon will not.

sections.title: Joab's Third Murder and Sheba's Pursuit
sections.commentary:
The pattern of Joab's career is now established: when his position is threatened, he kills. Amasa's appointment as army commander was presumably intended to demote Joab, and Joab's response is immediate and lethal.
